💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that powerful laser pulses could transform the crystal structure of a metal without first heating its atoms.
  • In a recent development, in a study published in Physical Review Materials, researchers led by Dr.
  • When an intense laser pulse strikes a metal, its electrons absorb energy far more rapidly than its atoms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that powerful laser pulses could transform the crystal structure of a metal without first heating its atoms. New research suggests that rapidly exciting electrons can make entirely different atomic arrangements energetically favorable, revealing an alternative way to control the structure and properties of metals.

In a recent development, in a study published in Physical Review Materials, researchers led by Dr. Sam Azadi modeled 17 elemental metals exposed to extreme electronic temperatures. Nearly all were predicted to undergo one or more solid-to-solid phase transitions driven by electronic excitation, potentially within a fraction of a picosecond (one trillionth of a second).

When an intense laser pulse strikes a metal, its electrons absorb energy far more rapidly than its atoms. This creates a temporary state in which the electrons reach extremely high temperatures while the atomic lattice remains relatively cold.

Sources indicate that under these conditions, a phenomenon known as electronic entropy can determine which crystal structure is most stable. Electronic entropy describes how electrons are distributed among available energy states. As electronic temperatures rise, changes in this distribution can alter the relative stability of competing crystal structures without requiring conventional heating of the atomic lattice.

In a recent development, “Our results suggest that electronic entropy should be regarded as a thermodynamic control parameter in its own right. Just as external pressure can transform one crystal structure into another, strong electronic excitation can reshape the free-energy landscape and create entirely upcoming phases of matter,” noted Dr. Sam Azadi, Research Associate in Theoretical Physics.

Using advanced computer simulations, the researchers calculated how increasing electronic temperatures affect the free energy of metals, a thermodynamic quantity that helps determine which structures are most stable. They identified transitions involving several common crystal arrangements, including hexagonal close-packed (hcp), face-centered cubic (fcc), and body-centered cubic (bcc) structures.

Sources indicate that in general, hotter electrons favored crystal structures with lower densities. The researchers attributed this tendency to electronic thermal pressure, which arises as electrons gain energy.

Some metals, however, displayed more complex behavior. Differences in the distribution of electronic states near the Fermi level, an notable energy reference in metals, can influence which atomic arrangements become favorable under intense excitation.

The predicted transitions occur on femtosecond to picosecond timescales, making them potential targets for experiments using ultrafast X-ray or electron diffraction. These techniques could allow scientists to track changes in atomic arrangements immediately after laser excitation and test the theoretical predictions.

Industry observers note that if confirmed experimentally, the findings could enable researchers to use carefully controlled laser pulses to temporarily switch metals between crystal structures, accessing material properties that are difficult to achieve under ordinary conditions. Such capabilities could have applications in ultrafast electronics, high-energy physics, and advanced manufacturing.

Sources indicate that reference: “Electronic-entropy-driven solid-solid phase transitions in elemental metals” by S. Azadi, S. M. Vinko, A. Principi, T. D. Kühne and M. S. Bahramy, 9 April 2026, Physical Review Materials. DOI: 10.1103/nzv9-dskm.

  • Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family revealed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family revealed.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

“Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

When McDermott declared his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

Recent findings suggest that he attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

In a recent development, he continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against newly introduced sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a newly introduced life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

In a recent development, as he stated, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Sources indicate that then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he noted in a statement at the time.

In a recent development, mcDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

Industry observers note that “Jim McDermott was as massive as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

Breaking: Researchers Have Discovered a Previously Unknown Crystal Form of Silver

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have discovered a previously unknown crystal structure of silver that exhibits unusually high chemical reactivity.
  • In a recent development, silver can take on an extraordinarily rare atomic structure that makes it far more chemically reactive than its familiar form.
  • The findings, published in Nano Letters, emerged when scientists used an electron beam to break down silver iodide and observed the resulting silver crystals at the atomic scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have discovered a previously unknown crystal structure of silver that exhibits unusually high chemical reactivity.

In a recent development, silver can take on an extraordinarily rare atomic structure that makes it far more chemically reactive than its familiar form. Researchers at Hokkaido University have discovered a previously unknown crystal arrangement in which silver atoms form a simple cubic pattern, a structure previously documented in only one other element.

The findings, published in Nano Letters, emerged when scientists used an electron beam to break down silver iodide and observed the resulting silver crystals at the atomic scale. Unlike ordinary silver, the newly formed crystals began converting into silver oxide within approximately 100 seconds, demonstrating how dramatically atomic arrangement can influence a material’s chemical behavior.

It has been revealed that most silver crystallizes in a structure known as face-centered cubic, in which atoms occupy the eight corners and the center of each face of a repeating cube. This tightly packed arrangement is also found in common metals such as gold, copper, and aluminum.

It has been revealed that the newly discovered silver instead formed a simple cubic structure, with atoms occupying only the corners of each repeating cube. This arrangement is exceptionally uncommon in pure elements. Before this discovery, the only known elemental example was radioactive polonium, whose simple cubic structure was identified in 1966.

Recent findings suggest that “It was surprising to find that such a low-density structure could form in a pure metal crystal,” claims first author Dr. Masaya Sakakibara. “We expected silver nanoparticles to form when silver iodide decomposes under electron beam irradiation, but we didn’t expect them to adopt a simple cubic structure.”.

The researchers created and examined the silver using a transmission electron microscope (TEM), which employs electrons with wavelengths shorter than those of visible light to resolve structures down to individual atoms. The electron beam served two purposes: it triggered the decomposition of silver iodide and allowed the scientists to watch the resulting silver atoms organize into crystals.

The nanoscale conditions were essential to the discovery. At dimensions of just a few billionths of a meter, materials can temporarily adopt crystal structures that would be unstable in larger samples. Such arrangements can produce physical and chemical properties that differ substantially from those of the same element in its conventional form.

According to recent reports, experiments conducted under high vacuum revealed a striking difference between the two silver structures. Conventional face-centered cubic silver remained stable, while the simple cubic crystals gradually oxidized, forming silver oxide. The rapid transformation provided direct evidence of the new structure’s unusually high chemical reactivity.

“Within 100 seconds of its formation, it began to transform into silver oxide,” adds Sakakibara.

The researchers believe their technique could provide a way to discover other previously unknown crystal structures and investigate the properties they produce.

“This is a new approach to discovering previously unknown crystal structures, which could also help us develop materials with novel properties in the future,” claims Professor Yuki Kimura, co-author of the study and head of the Low Temperature Nanomaterial Science Laboratory at Hokkaido University.

“Going forward, we will continue investigating the physical and chemical properties of simple cubic silver in greater detail and extend this approach to other elements and compounds.”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Electron-Beam-Assisted Formation of Simple-Cubic Silver” by Masaya Sakakibara, Hiroki Nada, Yuji Kunisada, Tomoya Yamazaki and Yuki Kimura, 4 November 2026, Nano Letters. DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c03635.

  • Latest research challenges a long-standing theory of how the inner ear detects sound, revealing a more complex process than previously understood.

  • For decades, scientists have understood the cochlea, the spiral-shaped structure inside the inner ear, as a frequency map.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest research challenges a long-standing theory of how the inner ear detects sound, revealing a more complex process than previously understood.

Scientists have discovered that low-frequency sounds can produce nearly simultaneous vibrations across widely separated regions of the inner ear. The finding, observed in guinea pigs, challenges a long-standing model of how hearing works and could influence the development of more advanced cochlear implants.

For decades, scientists have understood the cochlea, the spiral-shaped structure inside the inner ear, as a frequency map. Different sounds activate different locations along its membrane, much like individual piano keys correspond to specific notes. High frequencies stimulate one end, while low frequencies primarily activate the other. This arrangement, known as the “place code,” has helped explain how the ear distinguishes sounds and forms a foundation of modern cochlear implant technology.

Industry observers note that the traditional model dates back to research by Georg von Békésy, who received the 1961 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for demonstrating how different sound frequencies stimulate distinct regions of the cochlea. However, the new study, published in Science Advances, suggests that this location-based explanation does not fully account for how the inner ear processes low-frequency sounds.

Industry observers note that to investigate, researchers used optical coherence tomography (OCT), an imaging technology (co-invented by OHSU physician-scientist David Huang) widely used in eye examinations. Combined with advanced signal processing to reduce background noise, the technique allowed scientists to detect extremely small vibrations at multiple locations inside the guinea pig cochlea.

The measurements showed that low-frequency sounds produced similar vibrations across distant regions, often with synchronized motion. Rather than disproving the cochlea’s frequency map, the findings indicate that additional mechanisms may contribute to how low-frequency information is represented and interpreted. The results build on earlier research published in 2022 that identified unexpected patterns of low-frequency responses.

Industry observers note that understanding low-frequency hearing is particularly key for interpreting complex sounds, including speech. These vibrations are difficult to measure experimentally, and people with hearing loss often struggle to understand conversations when background noise is present.

“When you bring in low-frequency background noise, it’s a very challenging environment for people with hearing loss,” mentioned George Burwood, Ph.D., the study’s lead author and a research instructor at Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU). “Also, the place code paradigm limits the interpretation of how mammals evolved to detect extremely complex signals, especially speech.”.

Current cochlear implants use electrodes to electrically stimulate different regions of the cochlea according to sound frequency. The fresh findings suggest that reproducing more of the natural cochlea’s complex vibration patterns might improve how these devices convey sound information.

According to recent reports, “Cochlear implants are geared to take advantage of a place code,” Burwood remarked. “Our study suggests the optimal pattern of stimulation by electrodes in a cochlear implant may be more complex than just where and how intensely it’s being stimulated.”.

According to recent reports, the findings also raise questions about how the auditory system separates frequencies when vibrations are distributed across multiple cochlear locations. Researchers suspect the brain may use information beyond the position of stimulation to distinguish certain sounds.

It has been revealed that “This discovery advances our basic understanding in how hearing works,” said Larry Trussell, Ph.D., director of the Oregon Hearing Research Center at OHSU. “The brain appears to have mechanisms that are able to differentiate frequencies without having a map or place code.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “Denoised vibrometry reveals noncanonical filtering at the apex of the cochlea” by George W. S. Burwood, Pierre Hakizimana, Karl Grosh, Wajiha Zaidi, Ruikang K. Wang, Alfred L. Nuttall and Anders Fridberger, 20 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aei4634.

The research at OHSU was supported by the National Institutes of Health through award R01DC00141-44.

Recent findings suggest that all research involving animal subjects at OHSU must be reviewed and approved by the university’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). The IACUC’s priority is to ensure the health and safety of animal research subjects. The IACUC also reviews procedures to ensure the health and safety of the people who work with the animals. No live animal work may be conducted at OHSU without IACUC approval.

Marcel Proust and madeleines are so intrinsically linked that in France, a madeleine de Proust has become a common expression used to describe a smell, sound, or taste that brings back old memories. Madeleines are small sponge cakes baked in molds shaped like seashells with the signature bump, la bosse, proudly protruding from the top. Freezing the pan and placing it on a hot sheet pan will make the bump pop even more!

Recent findings suggest that as much as I love a plain madeleine, I adore a citrus-scented one. My first madeleine, my Proustian moment, was not at a lovely Parisian pâtisserie. No, my family and I were visiting some of my mother’s friends in Paris and not knowing what they were, I grabbed a bag of lemon madeleines in a local supermarket, simply because I thought the seashell-shaped cakes were the prettiest thing I had ever seen. I could have inhaled them all in an afternoon if I had been allowed.

Recent findings suggest that seasonal citrus zests—lemons, of course, yuzus, blood oranges, mandarins, or a medley of several—find their way into my madeleines, but the tart-sweet, fruity, floral flavor of Cara Cara oranges is my favorite. Dusting the still-warm madeleines with floral and citrusy coriander-scented powdered sugar just before serving sends them over the top.

More bright citrus recipes this way.

40 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

Industry observers note that put ½ cup / 115 g unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat and melt, stirring and scraping the bottom with a rubber spatula, until the foaming subsides and the butter smells like toasted hazelnuts and the milk solids are golden brown, 5–7 minutes. Scrape the melted butter and milk solids into a small heatproof bowl and refrigerate until the butter is solid and creamy.

It has been revealed that sift together 1 cup / 125 g all-purpose flour, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ¼ tsp. salt in a small bowl and set aside.

Add ½ cup / 100 g light brown sugar to a small bowl and rub the sugar with zest of 1 Cara Cara orange. Combine the sugar, 1 Tbsp. honey, and 2 eggs in the bowl of a stand mixer, fitted with the whisk attachment. Whisk for 2 minutes on medium-low speed, then increase the speed to medium-high and whisk for another 5–6 minutes, until very pale and airy.

Add the cooled butter to the egg mixture while whisking on low speed, then fold in the flour mixture until just combined.

Transfer the batter to an airtight container and refrigerate for at least 6 hours but preferably overnight.

Grease a madeleine pan with unsalted butter, then dust with all-purpose flour and knock out any excess. Place the pan in the freezer for at least an hour.

In a recent development, use a 1-Tbsp. measure or transfer the cold batter to a piping bag and fill the center of each cup with 20 g of batter (three-quarters full, or a little more than 1 Tbsp.). Refrigerate the madeleine pan for 1 hour.

Place a sheet pan in the oven and preheat the oven to 350°F / 180°C.

Place the madeleine pan directly on the hot sheet pan and bake for 10–13 minutes, until the madeleines are golden brown and their signature bump springs back when pressed lightly.

Tap the tray to release the cakes and immediately turn out onto a wire rack to cool, turning them bump-side up.

Whisk together ¼ cup / 30 g powdered sugar and ¾ tsp. ground coriander in a small bowl and dust over the warm madeleines.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a clinical trial led by researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF), people who took a standardized kudzu extract before anticipated episodes of heavy drinking experienced significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those given a placebo.
  • The findings, published in the American Journal of Psychiatry on November 4, suggest that taking a treatment during periods of heightened risk could offer a upcoming strategy for managing problematic alcohol consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A supplement derived from kudzu, a plant used for centuries in traditional East Asian medicine, may help people with alcohol use disorder reduce binge drinking without taking medication every day.

In a clinical trial led by researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF), people who took a standardized kudzu extract before anticipated episodes of heavy drinking experienced significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those given a placebo. The benefits persisted for three months after participants stopped taking the supplement.

The findings, published in the American Journal of Psychiatry on November 4, suggest that taking a treatment during periods of heightened risk could offer a upcoming strategy for managing problematic alcohol consumption.

Binge drinking accounts for more than half of the roughly 80,000 annual U.S. deaths attributed to excessive alcohol consumption. Despite the scale of the problem, fewer than 10% of people with alcohol use disorder have ever received medication to treat the condition.

“Binge drinking is incredibly common, but we don’t have many tools to offer people who want to cut back,” remarked Glenn-Milo Santos, PhD, MPH, the study’s lead author and a UCSF professor of community health systems. “Our goal is to expand that toolkit. What’s exciting about this approach is that people can use it when they know they may be at risk of heavy drinking, rather than taking a medication every day.”.

The trial involved 120 adults with alcohol use disorder who engaged in binge drinking at least once a week. Binge drinking was defined as consuming at least five alcoholic drinks on a single occasion for men and at least four for women.

Participants were divided into two groups, with half receiving a standardized kudzu extract and the other half receiving a placebo. Over 12 weeks, they were instructed to take their assigned treatment approximately 2.5 hours before they anticipated drinking heavily. Everyone also received brief weekly counseling sessions.

It has been revealed that by the end of the trial, participants taking kudzu had reduced their average number of binge-drinking days from 2.15 to 1.42 per week. Those receiving the placebo showed little improvement, with their weekly average declining from 2.15 to 2.06 days.

Recent findings suggest that kudzu also reduced how frequently participants experienced weeks involving any binge drinking. The proportion of such weeks dropped from 88% to 58% among those taking the extract, compared with a decline from 88% to 81% in the placebo group.

According to recent reports, three months after the treatment period ended, participants who had received kudzu continued to report significantly fewer binge-drinking days than those in the placebo group. Researchers suggest that drinking less during the trial may have helped participants reconsider their drinking habits and develop greater confidence in their ability to control their alcohol consumption.

Participants tolerated the kudzu extract well, experiencing no more side effects than those receiving the placebo. No serious adverse effects were linked to the treatment.

In a recent development, however, the researchers caution against assuming that commercially available kudzu supplements will deliver comparable benefits. The trial used a standardized formulation, whereas the composition of products sold over the counter can vary considerably. Larger clinical studies are needed to confirm the results across more diverse populations.

Reference: “Targeted Use of Kudzu for Binge Drinking Among Adults With Alcohol Use Disorder: A Phase 2b Randomized Trial” by Glenn-Milo Santos, Phillip Coffin, Allie Dunham, Thomas Hoffmann, John Walker, Tim Matheson and Steven Batki, 3 November 2026, American Journal of Psychiatry. DOI: 10.1176/appi.ajp.20251354.

This study was funded by National Institutes for Health (R01AA025930). Santos is also supported by a K24 career development grant from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), which is part of the NIH.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have identified a previously unknown group of aging immune cells that may undermine the body’s natural defenses.

Some aging immune cells do more than lose their ability to fight disease. Researchers at Monash University have identified a previously unknown group of immune cells that actively suppress the body’s defenses, potentially helping explain why cancer and serious infections become more common with age.

The discovery comes from a preclinical study published in Science Immunology. Using mouse models, scientists mapped genetic changes that cause immune cells to deteriorate in different ways, identifying potential targets for treatments aimed at preserving immune function later in life.

The researchers investigated CD8+ T cells, immune cells responsible for recognizing and destroying infected and cancerous cells. They identified three distinct ways aging disrupts the genetic programs controlling these cells, impairing their ability to respond to unfamiliar threats, regulate immune activity, and maintain normal cellular health.

According to recent reports, “Aging is the biggest risk factor for cancer overall,” mentioned Dr. Daniel Thiele, the study’s first author at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute. “Our immune system is constantly surveying our bodies for potentially cancerous cells and eliminating them, often without us ever knowing.”.

“As we age, this natural defense system becomes less effective, making us more vulnerable to cancer and infections and reducing our ability to respond to vaccines.”.

“This study provides a blueprint of immune aging, from which we can now identify potential targets to reverse aspects of that decline.”.

According to recent reports, the findings challenge the idea that immune cells simply become progressively weaker as they age. Some lose their protective functions, while others develop the ability to interfere with neighboring immune cells. These different patterns can occur within the same aging individual.

According to recent reports, “Even within the same aging individual, we found that immune cells can age in remarkably different ways,” Dr. Thiele noted. “Some cells lose their ability to protect us against disease, while others begin to interfere with the body’s own immune defenses.”.

“By understanding what goes wrong within these cells, we can begin to identify more targeted ways to restore immune function as we age.”.

Sources indicate that the research has also contributed to a separate discovery involving granzyme K, a protein produced by immune cells. In that study, Monash scientists identified granzyme K as a driver of age-related organ damage in mice, suggesting that changes in immune cell behavior may affect tissues beyond the immune system itself.

According to recent reports, the findings raise the possibility of developing therapies that address specific mechanisms of immune aging rather than attempting to stimulate the entire immune system. Such treatments remain a future prospect, with the current evidence coming from preclinical research.

“By understanding what drives aging within our immune cells, we may ultimately be able to target not only immune aging, but aging throughout the body,” said Professor Nicole La Gruta, the study’s senior researcher at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute.

Reference: “Aging drives distinct chromatin signatures of CD8 T cell dysfunction and the emergence of a unique CD8 Treg cell population” by Daniel Thiele, Liam C. Kealy, David Chisanga, Brendan E. Russ, Angela Nguyen, Jessica Runting, Iona S. Schuster, Adele Barugahare, Tabinda Hussain, Mohammad Asadian, Minh Bui, Taylah J. Bennett, Nemo Shindo, Justin B. Zhang, Jasmine Li, Mariapia A. Degli-Esposti, Axel Kallies, Kim Good-Jacobson, Colby Zaph, Stephen J. Turner and Nicole L. La Gruta, 20 November 2026, Science Immunology. DOI: 10.1126/sciimmunol.aej5412.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A red dwarf still circles the burned-out core of a star that could once have swallowed it, and their orbit is wider than astronomers expected.
  • A planet too faint to see can still give itself away by making the star it orbits wobble.
  • “We were actually looking for planets,” said lead author Étienne Artigau, a researcher at Université de Montréal’s Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A red dwarf still circles the burned-out core of a star that could once have swallowed it, and their orbit is wider than astronomers expected.

A planet too faint to see can still give itself away by making the star it orbits wobble. Astronomers looking for planets around a dim red star 28 light-years from Earth measured a wobble more than a thousand times larger than they expected. Following that motion revealed a family of three stars, two of which had already run out of fuel.

“We were actually looking for planets,” said lead author Étienne Artigau, a researcher at Université de Montréal’s Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx). “Instead, we found something much more surprising.”.

Industry observers note that the star they were watching was a red dwarf, a star much dimmer than the Sun. At the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi, a planet-hunting instrument called SPIRou (SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge) picked up a change of nearly 16 kilometers (10 miles) per second in the star’s speed. After several years of follow-up observations, the team knew that whatever was tugging on the red dwarf had more than half the Sun’s mass.

“The unusual combination of high mass and very low brightness left only one plausible explanation: it was the remnant of a dead star,” said Charles-Antoine Parent, an undergraduate student at Université Laval and co-author of the study. “The most likely explanation was a white dwarf, although a neutron star or even a black hole couldn’t be ruled out.”.

The team finally saw the faint companion with Gemini North, another telescope on Maunakea. High-resolution images from its ʻAlopeke instrument showed a white dwarf orbiting the red dwarf. A white dwarf is the extremely dense core a star leaves behind after it runs out of fuel. Most stars, including the Sun, will end their lives this way.

Industry observers note that astronomers already knew about a white dwarf much farther out. That outer star circles both the red dwarf and its newly spotted companion. No other trio like this one, named Welopōʻai, is known within 100 light-years of Earth.

Before it became a white dwarf, the red dwarf’s closer neighbor was about 40 percent more massive than the Sun. As it aged, it swelled into a giant several hundred times its original size. The red dwarf would have been close enough for the expanding giant to affect it. In similar systems, a giant can swallow its companion, and the two stars can even merge. Welopōʻai’s red dwarf appears to have survived. It now circles the remnant in a stable orbit, farther away than astronomers would expect given how close the two once were.

Sources indicate that “This system should not exist,” said Patrick Dufour, a professor at Université de Montréal who studies white dwarfs and co-authored the paper. “We have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.”.

According to recent reports, the team wants to find out whether the pull of all three stars on one another could explain the inner pair’s orbit. The researchers also measured the inner white dwarf’s mass with an uncertainty of less than 1 percent. Astronomers rarely get such a precise mass for a white dwarf, and it gives them a way to test predictions about how stars age and how matter behaves when packed so tightly together. The international team, led by IREx, reported its in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

The simulation illustrates how gravitational interactions between its three stars could influence their orbits over time. The sonification translates the stars’ orbital motions into sound, so you can hear the system’s changing rhythms. Credit: Heidi White (UMONTREAL/IREx). Simulation data: Alexandre Correia, University of Coimbra.

In a recent development, welopōʻai got its name through A Hua He Inoa (“To Call Forth a Name”), a program of the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi. The name joins welo, an inherited or family trait, with pōʻai, an orbit or circular path. Together they evoke a “path of family traits.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,” Artigau mentioned. “Even when we’re searching for planets, our Universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My earliest dessert obsession was the malted milkshake, which I indulged in every time I had enough babysitting money. My oldest, best friend, Toi, was equally obsessed with Whoppers, and we both wondered why malted sweets were so good. Turns out, the secret is in the combination of malted barley, wheat flour, and evaporated whole milk that gets toasted to caramelize the sugars contained in it.

This cake is my latest malted creation. Layering the malted vanilla and chocolate batters so they create a striped pattern isn’t just an aesthetic choice. Doing so really does keep the flavors distinct. Starting off in a cold oven allows the cake to bake evenly without overbrowning and results in a smooth, fine, melt-in your-mouth crumb. For extra malted flavor, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with malted vanilla syrup in several additions, letting the syrup sink in after each addition.

Industry observers note that I originally made this syrup to give my milkshakes that nostalgic, malt-shop flavor. But honey, it’s no one-hit wonder. It is a beautiful sweetener and is terrific when brushed on top of still-warm Striped Malted Pound Cake.

It has been revealed that I also drizzle it over roasted fruit and mix it into buttercreams, glazes, and frostings. For breakfast, I stir it into coffee or lattes, smoothies, yogurt, and oatmeal. And it’s got savoy game, too. Try it on a dinner plate, spooned over roasted sweet potatoes or carrots alongside roasted chops or chicken.

More delicious loaf cake recipes this way.

Makes one 9x5" loaf, 12 to 16 servings.

Grease a 9x5" loaf pan with softened butter or cooking spray. Dust the pan with all-purpose flour, shaking out any excess.

In a medium bowl, whisk together 1¾ cups / 220g all-purpose flour, 1⁄4 cup / 34g cornstarch, 1⁄2 tsp. fine sea salt, and 1⁄2 tsp. baking powder.

Industry observers note that in a stand mixer fitted with the paddle, combine 16 Tbsp. / 2 sticks / 226g unsalted butter, at room temperature, 1¼ cups / 273g granulated sugar, and 1⁄4 cup / 37g malted milk powder. Beat, starting on low speed and increasing to medium-high speed until lightened in color and fluffy, 5–7 minutes, scraping down the sides of the bowl once or twice.

On medium-low speed, add 3 large eggs, at room temperature, one at a time, scraping down the sides of the bowl after each one is incorporated.

Add one-third of the flour mixture and beat on the lowest speed until just combined. Add 2 Tbsp. heavy cream and beat on low speed until just combined. Add another one-third of the flour mixture, beating until combined, and another 2 Tbsp. heavy cream to combine. Add the remaining one-third of the flour mixture and beat until the batter is smooth, scraping down the sides of the bowl as necessary. Mix in 1½ tsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract and 1½ tsp. whiskey or bourbon (if using).

Recent findings suggest that transfer 1½ cups of the batter to a medium bowl. Sift in 3 Tbsp. unsweetened cacao powder or cocoa powder and add the remaining 1⁄4 cup heavy cream, stirring to form a smooth chocolate batter.

To create the striped layers, drop 1 cup of the vanilla cake batter into the center of the loaf pan and then drop ½ cup of the chocolate batter on top of the vanilla batter. The alternating layers do not have to totally cover each other and let the layers spread naturally. Continue to drop those same-size portions of batter directly on top of each other, alternating the vanilla and chocolate, until all the batter is used. The batter should have spread to the corners, but if not, gently rap the pan on the counter to help it even out. Smooth the top with a small offset spatula.

Place the cake in a cold oven and set the temperature to 300°F. Bake until the loaf is golden, its top is slightly cracked, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 1 hour 20 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes.

According to recent reports, let the cake cool in the pan on a wire rack for 10 minutes, then run a knife around the edges to release it. Invert the cake onto a wire rack, reinvert, and cover the warm cake loosely in plastic wrap until completely cooled. If desired, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with ½ cup Malted Vanilla Syrup several times, letting the syrup sink in after each addition. The cake will keep, wrapped in plastic at room temperature, for up to 5 days.

In a recent development, in a small saucepan, combine ⅓ cup / 73g granulated sugar, ½ cup / 120g water, 2 Tbsp. malted milk powder, and pinch of fine sea salt. Cook over medium heat until bubbling, whisking until the sugar and malt powder dissolve and the mixture becomes glossy, slightly thickened, and evenly beige, 2–3 minutes.

Remove from heat and whisk in 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract. Let cool slightly before using. This will keep in a covered jar or airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

Scientists Discover That Jupiter and Dead Stars Could Hold Clues to Dark Matter’s Biggest Mystery

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The warmth of planets and dead stars is helping scientists narrow the possibilities for dark matter, offering fresh clues about the mysterious substance that makes up most of the universe’s matter.
  • Most of the matter in the universe is something scientists have never directly seen.
  • Sources indicate that scientists have spent decades searching for particles that could explain dark matter, without directly detecting any.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The warmth of planets and dead stars is helping scientists narrow the possibilities for dark matter, offering fresh clues about the mysterious substance that makes up most of the universe’s matter.

Most of the matter in the universe is something scientists have never directly seen. Known as dark matter, it is thought to make up about 85% of all matter, yet its true nature remains a mystery. Researchers know it exists largely because of its gravitational effects, but they still do not know what it is made of.

Sources indicate that scientists have spent decades searching for particles that could explain dark matter, without directly detecting any. One possibility is that some particles move so slowly that they barely register in laboratory experiments. However, those same particles might be easier to find in places much larger than any detector on Earth: planets and stars.

Sources indicate that researchers Alejandro Ibarra, Merlin Reichard, and Gaurav Tomar investigated whether these celestial bodies could act as natural traps for dark matter. Their study, published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics (JCAP), found no evidence of dark matter but helped rule out certain possibilities about its properties.

Sources indicate that dark matter is known to interact through gravity, but scientists suspect it may also have extremely weak electrical or magnetic properties. Some particles could carry a tiny electric charge or behave like miniature magnets, allowing them to interact with ordinary matter in ways that are difficult to detect.

Sources indicate that speed could make those interactions even harder to observe. When a slow-moving particle strikes material inside a detector, it may transfer too little energy to produce a measurable signal. Inside a planet or star, however, even a small loss of energy could be enough to prevent the particle from escaping the object’s gravitational pull.

Over billions of years, these trapped particles could accumulate near the center of a planet or star. If their properties allow it, they might eventually collide and undergo a process called annihilation, transforming into other particles. Some of the resulting particles could escape into space, while others could release energy that warms the surrounding material.

It has been revealed that “In this work, we considered four celestial bodies: Earth, the Sun, Jupiter and white dwarfs,” explains Gaurav Tomar, a researcher at the Center for Quantum Spacetime at Sogang University in South Korea and the study’s corresponding author. “There are dedicated experiments, for example IceCube at the South Pole, looking for neutrinos from the Sun and Earth. For Jupiter and white dwarfs, we considered the heating possibilities.”.

Sources indicate that the researchers used two different approaches to look for signs of dark matter. For Earth and the Sun, they examined existing searches for neutrinos, tiny particles that can travel through enormous amounts of matter without being stopped. If dark matter particles were annihilating deep inside these bodies, some of the resulting neutrinos might reach detectors and provide evidence of what was happening.

According to recent reports, for Jupiter and white dwarfs, which are dense remnants of stars, the team looked at heat instead. Unlike the Sun, these objects are not powered by ongoing nuclear fusion, making them potentially useful places to investigate whether another source of energy is contributing to their warmth.

The researchers calculated how much heat different types of dark matter could produce if captured inside these objects, then compared those predictions with the energy the objects actually emit. If a particular type of dark matter would generate more heat than an object releases, that scenario could be ruled out.

By combining these calculations with existing observations, the team excluded several combinations of dark matter particle mass and electromagnetic properties that previous experiments had not eliminated. Earth was particularly useful for investigating particles with extremely small electric charges, while white dwarfs helped constrain other possible electromagnetic interactions.

The findings also come with an notable uncertainty. How much dark matter a celestial body could capture depends partly on how much dark matter surrounds it. For white dwarfs in particular, researchers must rely on estimates because the local dark matter density is not always known.

“We do not know the dark matter density there. We used estimated values, so if those values change, our limits could become weaker or stronger,” Tomar notes.

In a recent development, he was referring to the M4 star cluster, where the white dwarfs examined in the study are located. The amount of dark matter in that region has not been directly measured and must instead be estimated using models.

Sources indicate that looking ahead, Tomar suggests searching for even colder white dwarfs in regions thought to contain more dark matter. Because these stars emit relatively little heat, any additional warming from trapped particles could be easier to identify. Planets orbiting stars beyond our solar system could also offer new opportunities to investigate whether dark matter is quietly accumulating inside celestial bodies.

In a recent development, reference: “Celestial probes of dark matter electromagnetic interactions” by Alejandro Ibarra, Merlin Reichard and Gaurav Tomar, August 27, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 2608.27957.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

In a recent development, while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever latest ideas have been simmering since last year’s massive meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

It has been revealed that stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Sources indicate that why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

According to recent reports, I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

It has been revealed that nobody indicates they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

This is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated promptly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be noted is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

NASA-Funded Study Reveals a Hidden Effect of Space Radiation on the Brain

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upcoming NASA-funded research reveals that cosmic radiation triggers subtle, sex-specific changes in the brain without causing immediate cognitive problems.
  • Cosmic radiation can change the brain’s immune cells in different ways in males and females, even when no obvious problems with memory or behavior appear.
  • It has been revealed that earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field shield people from much of the galactic cosmic radiation that fills space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming NASA-funded research reveals that cosmic radiation triggers subtle, sex-specific changes in the brain without causing immediate cognitive problems.

Cosmic radiation can change the brain’s immune cells in different ways in males and females, even when no obvious problems with memory or behavior appear. A new NASA-funded study in mice found distinct molecular responses to simulated space radiation, raising questions about how prolonged exposure could affect astronauts traveling to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

It has been revealed that earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field shield people from much of the galactic cosmic radiation that fills space. These highly energetic particles, often described as cosmic “rays,” can damage spacecraft electronics and potentially affect living tissue. Understanding their effects on the brain is a major concern for future missions beyond Earth’s protective magnetic field.

In a recent development, researchers at the University of Rochester exposed male and female mice to simulated galactic cosmic radiation at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory at Brookhaven National Laboratory. Led by neuroscience graduate student Mark Osabutey, MBChB, the team used single-cell RNA sequencing to examine nearly 16,000 microglia, the brain’s resident immune cells. This technique allowed scientists to investigate how radiation affected gene activity in individual cells.

The analysis, published in Scientific Reports, identified different molecular responses in males and females. Male microglia showed changes involving cellular stress adaptation and metabolism, while female microglia exhibited broader reductions in immune signaling pathways. Neither group showed widespread inflammatory activation or detectable radiation-related cognitive or behavioral impairment at the time of testing.

Recent findings suggest that “Surprisingly, despite clear molecular changes, we found no widespread inflammatory activation or measurable radiation-associated behavioral impairment at the time we examined,” said Osabutey. The findings suggest that cellular responses to radiation can occur without immediately producing measurable functional problems, although their longer-term effects remain unknown.

It has been revealed that despite these sex-specific differences, researchers identified one response shared by both groups. Levels of FKBP5, a protein involved in regulating cellular stress responses, increased in the cortex and dentate gyrus of male and female mice. These brain regions contribute to functions including cognition, learning, and memory.

Industry observers note that “We now need to understand whether FKBP5 plays a protective or harmful role, and how different radiation exposures and other spaceflight stressors influence long-term brain health,” said Osabutey. “Our findings highlight the importance of considering biological sex when assessing neurological risks during spaceflight and identify potential pathways for developing protective strategies.”.

Recent findings suggest that university of Rochester Professor of Neuroscience M. Kerry O’Banion, MD, PhD, has investigated the neurological effects of space radiation for more than 15 years. A member of the Del Monte Institute for Neuroscience, O’Banion previously contributed to research indicating that cosmic radiation could accelerate the onset of Alzheimer’s disease.

Industry observers note that “We know cognitive changes from exposure to radiation in space are a real risk,” O’Banion said. “It’s key we understand how brain cells are changed. Knowing which mechanisms are impacted and how may help the development of countermeasures to protect or lessen an astronaut’s exposure to space radiation.”.

In a recent development, the latest findings do not establish whether the observed immune cell changes are harmful, protective, or temporary. Researchers also cannot yet determine whether they contribute to neurological problems after prolonged exposure. “Additional studies examining other time points and effects in other experimental systems will be required to understand this further,” O’Banion remarked.

It has been revealed that osabutey has participated in NASA-funded research since joining O’Banion’s laboratory. In 2023, he received a NASA predoctoral grant augmentation award to investigate changes in microglial populations following exposure to galactic cosmic radiation. He has also presented the laboratory’s research at a NASA conference and attended the European Space Agency Summer School in Darmstadt, Germany.

“Receiving NASA support has allowed me to contribute to research addressing questions of national and international importance,” mentioned Osabutey. “As a physician-scientist in training, I could not have asked for a better environment in which to train, and the experience has taught me how to pursue meaningful scientific questions through rigorous basic/translational investigation and collaboration, skills that I will carry forward in my future efforts to better understand brain injury and neurological disease.”.

The research involved a broader collaboration between University of Rochester scientists and personnel at Brookhaven National Laboratory, where particle accelerators generate radiation conditions relevant to spaceflight.

“Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows have been an essential part of our NASA research effort,” O’Banion said. “It’s comprised of a large team that includes the outstanding organizational skills of our long-time senior research technician, Lee Trojanczyk, as well as support personnel at Brookhaven National Labs. Over time, nearly a dozen University of Rochester trainees have contributed to this work.”.

Industry observers note that reference: “Single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals sex-specific microglial responses to simulated galactic cosmic radiation without broad inflammatory activation” by Mark A. Osabutey, Lia Calcines-Rodríguez, Lee A. Trojanczyk, John A. Olschowka and M. Kerry O’Banion, 20 November 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-77661-9.

This research was supported by a NASA grant and a NASA Human Research Program Grant Augmentation Award.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most key restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

Sources indicate that we enhancement this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he rolled out Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.
