A Train Carrying Deadly Materials Was on Fire for Nearly an Hour as It Barreled Toward a Small Town. Why Didn’t Anyone Stop It?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that editor’s note: In July 2024, after this story was published, the National Transportation Safety Board released its final analysis on the Norfolk Southern freight train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio.
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • Sources indicate that on the frigid evening of Friday, February 3, 2023, at around 8:50 p.m., a Norfolk Southern freight train measuring more than a mile and three quarters long snaked its way through the town of East Palestine, Ohio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that editor’s note: In July 2024, after this story was published, the National Transportation Safety Board released its final analysis on the Norfolk Southern freight train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio. It also released a companion illustrated digest of the incident. The analysis determined that the train derailed after an overheated wheel bearing caused an axel to “burn off.” The punctured DOT-111 tank car leaked butyl acrylates, which are flammable and likely started the post-derailment fires. Further, the decision to intentionally “vent and burn” vinyl chloride tank cars was likely unnecessary and based on incomplete or misleading information, according to the report. The NTSB issued 34 fresh safety recommendations covering several needs, including defect detection systems, tank car standards, hazardous materials, and emergency response procedures.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Sources indicate that on the frigid evening of Friday, February 3, 2023, at around 8:50 p.m., a Norfolk Southern freight train measuring more than a mile and three quarters long snaked its way through the town of East Palestine, Ohio. The train consisted of 149 cars, pulled by three locomotives—two at the front, one in the middle—and traveled just under 50 miles per hour. Of those 149 cars, 20 were tankers labeled with hazardous-materials placards. Several of the tankers contained liquefied vinyl chloride gas, the combustible and carcinogenic precursor material for PVC pipe; others contained ethylene glycol, a toxic ingredient in antifreeze. Driving the lead locomotive was Tony Faison, the train’s engineer; with him were the train’s conductor and a trainee.

In a recent development, engineers chart their progress by designated mile markers along the track. About 20 minutes earlier, the train had crossed mile marker 69.0, just east of Salem, Ohio. While crossing that spot, an infrared sensor built into the track called a “hotbox detector” had reported elevated temperatures on one of the front axles of the 23rd railcar. The ambient temperature that night was 10 degrees Fahrenheit. The bearings on the axle had reached an abnormally hot temperature of 103. The car, a hopper designed to hold commodities like grain, wasn’t carrying hazardous materials, but the hotbox detector relayed an alert to Norfolk Southern’s Atlanta command center all the same. No further action was taken.

As the train left East Palestine, it approached Ohio’s border with Pennsylvania, passing within a few hundred feet of the State Line Tavern, a local watering hole. There, at 8:55 p.m., it crossed mile marker 49.8. As the twenty-third car crossed the next hotbox detector, the infrared sensors revealed that the temperature of the axle’s bearings had risen sharply, to over 250 degrees. Faison immediately received an audio message from the locomotive’s onboard computer to stop the train. He reacted quickly to apply the brakes, but it was too late. He didn’t know it, but for the previous 40 minutes, his train had been on fire.

The train took more than a thousand feet to come to a stop. As it did, the compromised axle gave way. The left-side journal box, which held the axle in place, broke off and landed on one side of the track; the wheelset, consisting of the axle with two steel wheels mounted at both ends, ended up on the other. The twenty-third car jumped the rail, and the cars behind it followed suit, creating a tremendous series of crashes that could be heard throughout town. Thirty-eight railcars piled up, including 11 of the hazmat tankers.

Faison leaped from the locomotive to inspect the damage. From his standpoint at the front of the train, he could see flames rising into the night. He immediately contacted 911. So did many of the town’s residents, reporting both the train crash and the fire. One thought a gas station had exploded.

In the next few hours, the toxic flames would force an evacuation of the town. The specter of chemical poisoning lingered over East Palestine for months. And even today, the question of how a system of detectors—expressly designed to prevent this kind of derailment—failed to notice a dangerously overheated train axle remains unanswered.

It has been revealed that in the minutes after the derailment, first responders rushed to the blaze, but they were initially underequipped. Serving a town of fewer than five thousand people, the East Palestine fire department was a mostly volunteer force. The sole professional on staff was Chief Keith Drabick, who on that night was almost three hundred miles away, driving through Pennsylvania on vacation. Informed of the crash at 9 p.m., Drabick turned his car around and drove straight back to East Palestine, but he didn’t arrive until five hours later. For the first few minutes, volunteers had to fight the blaze alone. Meanwhile, following protocol, Faison cut the first two locomotives from the train and moved them a mile down the track. In the confusion that followed, some firefighters seemed unaware they were responding to a hazmat site and reported to residents that the burning train cars were carrying only malt liquor.

In a recent development, some of the train cars were carrying malt liquor, but others contained stronger stuff. As the scope of the disaster slowly became clear, the volunteers were joined by professional firefighting crews from nearby counties, including a special hazmat squad. At 9:45 p.m., concerned about the risks of a vinyl chloride explosion as well as the toxic cocktail of flaming chemicals escaping into the night, officials began evacuating nearby homes. Meanwhile, some of the contents of the leaking tankers began seeping into nearby Sulphur Run, a stream that flowed directly from the crash site through the center of town.

According to recent reports, even before the official order, citizens had started to evacuate. East Palestine resident Jami Wallace had learned of the train wreck from her mother. Wallace, a human resources manager in her forties, had recently gotten engaged. She called her fiancé, who was with a friend at the State Line Tavern. Driving past the burning crash site, he raced home to collect Wallace and their three-year-old daughter. “Grabbed her a couple of changes of clothes and out the door we went,” she told me. “We didn’t even know where we were going. It was the middle of winter and the heater was broken in the car.”.

After an hour and a half of firefighting, the Ohio State Police expanded the evacuation zone to one mile surrounding the derailment site. Around midnight, still fearing an explosion, the firefighters retreated. They then began to survey the crash site with aerial drones, in an attempt to determine which specific chemicals were leaking. The survey was challenging: The site was, well, a train wreck, and some of the plastic hazardous-materials placards had melted in the fire.

Eventually, responders determined that three hazmat cars had been physically breached. One contained ethylene glycol, the antifreeze ingredient, which can be lethal in concentrated doses. The other two contained acrylates, used as base ingredients in adhesives and paint. All three materials were burning off, releasing volatile organic compounds into the air. The fire was additionally fueled by nonhazardous but flammable railcar cargo, including several tankers loaded with petroleum lubricants. For days to come, an ominous toxic cloud hung suspended over the site. “You know how smoke, like, moves through the sky? Yeah, this wasn’t moving anywhere,” Wallace remarked. “It was almost like a green cloud that was, like, hovering.”.

Initially, none of the vinyl chloride tankers were breached. (If they had been, a series of explosions might have occurred, and the cancer-causing chemical could have rained down on the town.) Still, five vinyl chloride tankers, containing more than 115,000 gallons of vinyl chloride in total, had piled up in the burn zone. Each tanker had an emergency pressure release valve designed to vent gas into the atmosphere. Over the next few days, as temperatures rose inside the tanks, these valves automatically opened and closed, periodically releasing excess vinyl chloride gas into the air—where it immediately caught fire. In one extraordinary display on the evening of Saturday, February 4, one of the tanker valves vented for 70 continuous minutes, creating a spectacular flamethrower.

Recent findings suggest that with the crash site cordoned off and the tankers burping flames, officials deliberated on what to do. One worry was that the release valves on the tankers were starting to suffer thermal damage. Another was that the vinyl chloride inside the tanks might “polymerize,” forming into chains of PVC, which might cause the valves to stick, sealing the pressure in and causing the tankers to blow.

Industry observers note that from the outside, the hazmat experts couldn’t be sure if polymerization was occurring. Eventually they settled on two options. One option was to deliberately puncture the tanks and conduct a controlled burn of the vinyl chloride gas. The other option was to wait it out and hope the tanks cooled down enough so they wouldn’t explode. Chief Drabick was presented with this devil’s bargain: Wait, and potentially watch the exploding tanks rain shrapnel and poisonous chemicals on his town, or release mass quantities of vinyl chloride—a known Group A carcinogen—into the atmosphere. “I was given 13 minutes to make a decision,” Drabick told investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the federal agency responsible for investigating the wreck.

In a recent development, after consulting with his chief officers, Drabick chose to vent and burn. Following an expanded evacuation order, specialists attached explosive charges to the exteriors of five damaged tanker cars. At 4:37 p.m. on February 6, the charges were detonated, sending twin columns of flaming vinyl chloride gas high into the air and obscuring the setting sun with thick, black smoke. The burn continued through the following day; it was not until February 8, five days after the axle on train car 23 had first started to burn, that the fire was fully put out.

East Palestine soon found itself host to another kind of toxic cocktail, one consisting of corporate communications specialists, blustering public officials, government bureaucrats, and enterprising class-action attorneys. Complementing this splendid company were the more respectable representatives of the NTSB. Leading the agency’s efforts was Ruben Payan, an NTSB veteran with a heavy build, a thick mustache, and a calm and measured voice. Under his patient command, the NTSB began a thorough investigation of the crash site and the events leading up to the derailment.

The agency published the first investigation enhancement to its website in March 2023. And then on June 22, Payan presented his preliminary results at a public meeting in East Palestine. (It was the first onsite NTSB meeting in six years.) Using security camera footage collected from homes and businesses adjacent to the tracks, Payan was able to present a detailed videography of the train’s final minutes. Between the towns of Sebring and East Palestine, more than a dozen surveillance cameras had captured the train in motion; in ten of those camera feeds, the train was plainly on fire. In true-color camera feeds, the lower axle of the twenty-third car glowed a dull orange color; in infrared camera feeds, it blazed an intense white, throwing visible sparks.

The first two cameras to show the fire were in Salem, Ohio, some 26 miles west of East Palestine. The train passed the first camera at 8:11 p.m., 44 minutes before the derailment. That camera, which overlooked an alley of snow-covered cars, caught the train in the far background, its axle glowing orange. The camera was located six miles in front of the Salem hotbox detector—the one that had sent an alert to Atlanta but did not stop the train.

How had the Salem hotbox detector missed the fire? The cameras clearly showed flames and sparks along the length of the bottom of the twenty-third car, but when that same car crossed the hotbox detector 10 minutes later, infrared sensors registered the bearing temperatures at only 103 degrees. This wasn’t a case of a sputtering fire that started and stopped, either—the cameras along the route showed a steady blaze. The NTSB declined to comment for this story, citing the pending results of the final investigation. Norfolk Southern declined to comment as well.

It has been revealed that I put the question to David Farwick, a veteran engineer who commanded trains in Ohio for Norfolk Southern for nearly 40 years. He told me that Norfolk Southern’s systems were well maintained and up to date. “Those hotbox detectors, they’re pretty sensitive,” he said. “It’s not like we were working with 1960s stuff. They were pretty good.” The detectors are positioned among the crossties on the track and use infrared sensors to scan the undercarriage of the train. More than 6,000 are deployed across North America. The sensors on the hotbox detectors line up directly with the roller bearings. Farwick seemed flabbergasted that a flaming train had crossed a detector and not tripped an immediate brake alert. “It blows my mind,” he said.

Regulators have also grown concerned in recent years about how long the trains are getting. Farwick told me trains are growing so long that engineers have trouble seeing the backs of them, even on a curve. I asked him whether the train crew would have known they were carrying hazardous materials. “Absolutely,” he mentioned. Farwick explained that the conductor on each train carries a bound paper manifest of the train’s cargo known as a “consist.” In the event of a derailment or crash, a hard copy of this consist is to be immediately delivered to first responders. But Drabick, when questioned by NTSB investigators, said his firefighters never received the consist directly from the Norfolk Southern train crew: “I do not believe that we had any contact with those individuals,” he said. Drabick was only fully informed of the train’s hazardous contents when he arrived on site hours later.

The other looming question about the crash involves the degree of environmental poisoning East Palestine has suffered. In the months following the vent and burn of vinyl chloride gas, Environmental Protection Agency personnel repeatedly visited the town and surrounding areas to take soil samples. Per the EPA’s website, “the sample results indicate that impacts from the smoke and soot were minimal.” The EPA has also monitored the health of the town’s waterways. In the aftermath of the disaster, the agency recorded more than 40,000 dead fish and aquatic animals in the Sulphur Run creek adjacent to the derailment and burn site. While the agency claims that the creek “has not shown any contaminants at levels that exceed health standards since May 1,” it continues to maintain “Keep Out” signs posted around Sulphur Run.

East Palestine is immediately downstream of the crash site, and many local residents believe the creek has delivered poison into their homes. Two days after the derailment, Wallace returned to her evacuated residence to pick up some medication. “As soon as I pulled into my driveway, it hit me in the face—I started coughing ... until, like, I can’t breathe,” she said. “I look over because I know it’s the creek. I look over, and I see these chemicals free-floating down.”.

Wallace told me water from the creek regularly seeps into the basement of her residence, and that she has since relocated. She has pushed for the EPA to start indoor monitoring in East Palestine homes; so far, the agency has declined. In any case, the damages Norfolk Southern owes the town are substantial. In June, Norfolk Southern confirmed that cleanup costs and injury compensation settlements related to East Palestine would cost the manufacturer nearly $1 billion, though it anticipated that much of that cost would be covered by insurance.

In a statement a couple of weeks after the crash, Jennifer Homendy, the chair of the NTSB, described the accident as “100 percent preventable,” but didn’t offer specifics. She was likely referring to the “hot axle” phenomenon. Train axles use ring-shaped bearings that keep the axle secure while permitting it and the wheels to rotate. A skateboard’s wheels rotate using lubricated ball bearings inside the wheels. Train cars instead use cylindrical roller bearings, which make contact with the axle, permitting easy rotation.

As of December 2023, the NTSB has not yet made a final determination, but multiple experts I talked with told me that they believed a failed roller bearing was the most likely cause of the East Palestine derailment. About two dozen trains derail this way in North America every year. Bearings can fail for any number of reasons, including insufficient lubrication, contamination, overloading, and, simply, age. Once a bearing fails, the axle begins to grind against the metal, and this friction causes a rapid rise in temperature; this was potentially the source of the fire. “Bearings do break down, but that’s the reason why you get these detectors, right?” Farwick stated. “That’s exactly what these things are supposed to prevent.”.

The roller bearings on train axles are sealed inside the wheel and can’t readily be accessed. A faulty one can easily escape visual detection. Hotbox detectors, by using infrared temperature sensors to monitor the bearings in motion, offer a second layer of protection. Generally speaking, they work. Since the early 1980s, train derailments in North America have fallen from more than 7,000 annually to just over 1,000, in part because of hotbox detectors.

Recent findings suggest that the place to catch the failed roller bearing was not in East Palestine, but 20 miles west, in Salem, Ohio, where the train had crossed a detector 30 minutes before the derailment. That detector had recorded temperatures 93 degrees above the outside environment and sent a noncritical signal to Norfolk Southern central command in Atlanta. Whether dispatchers in Atlanta relayed this warning to the train crew remains unclear; the NTSB has yet to publish transcripts from the train’s black box recorder, and Norfolk Southern has refused to discuss the details of the accident.

Perhaps it is worth noting that in the days before the derailment, the East Palestine train had already been delayed twice by stops for unrelated mechanical concerns.

In March, the NTSB opened a probe into Norfolk Southern’s safety culture. Regulators were concerned not only by the East Palestine derailment, but also two other Ohio derailments in the surrounding months, as well as separate incidents in which three railroad workers on Norfolk Southern lines were killed in a span of 16 months, starting in December of 2021. In a statement announcing the investigation, the NTSB urged Norfolk Southern “to take immediate action today to review and assess its safety practices.”.

This October, Norfolk Southern unveiled a new layer of protection: giant metal sheds, festooned with cameras, that each train will pass through at various points on its journey. The shed is described as a “portal,” and its cameras take an average of 1,000 images per railcar, and send those images to an A.I. data center. Deep-learning algorithms are then employed to spot problems that track detectors and overworked railcar mechanics cannot.

Sources indicate that following the derailment, legislators introduced the bipartisan Railway Safety Act of 2023, which proposed decreasing the required distance between hotbox detectors to 15 miles, from an average of 25 miles today. The legislation is well intended, but it’s not clear if it would have prevented the East Palestine derailment: On that track, the hotbox detectors were an average of 16.7 miles apart. Closing the distance to 15 miles wouldn’t necessarily help.

It has been revealed that the most striking revelation from the NTSB’s preliminary findings was the sheer number of camera feeds that had captured the train car on fire. It costs about $200,000 to install a hotbox detector, and critics have estimated the cost of compliance for the Railway Safety Act at up to $2 billion. Perhaps wireless video cameras could permit dispatchers and AI to regularly monitor the status of the cars, and would give engineers better visibility to the back of the trains.

Finally, there’s still the problem of the toxic derailment site. It remains a hazard zone, and the nearby State Line Tavern remains closed. Under the guidance of the EPA, much of the topsoil near ground zero was excavated. The soil was supposed to be shipped to a hazardous waste facility in Oklahoma, but that state’s governor, Kevin Stitt, blocked the blueprint in March. Similarly, the contaminated water from Sulphur Run was drained. The water was supposed to be sent to a treatment facility in Baltimore, but that fell through too.

For a while, the poisoned water and soil remained at the derailment site. “They have these significant Shamu tanks,” Wallace stated. “They each hold, like, 100 million gallons of water.” Wallace said a neighbor had flown a drone over the tanks, and seen the chemical sheen on top. Nearby, the toxic dirt was piled into giant mounds, and covered with tarps.

In a recent development, however, as of January 2026, the EPA reported that personnel had completed a “site-wide cleanup and restoration,” in which crews cleaned the remaining oily sheens from nearby waterways such as Leslie and Sulphur Runs, and removed more than 38 million gallons of wastewater. They also removed any remaining contaminated soil and debris for treatment or disposal, and completed the derailment site excavation. The EPA is now sampling groundwater, surface water, and drinking water quarterly and will continue monitoring the area. Comprehensive updates of the work are available at the EPA’s website.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simplified ocean model highlights cooling only the far north drew nearly as much ice age carbon into the sea as cooling the whole planet.
  • In a recent development, the ice ages are known for the ice sheets that spread across the far north.
  • A upcoming modeling study suggests the two ends were connected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simplified ocean model highlights cooling only the far north drew nearly as much ice age carbon into the sea as cooling the whole planet.

In a recent development, the ice ages are known for the ice sheets that spread across the far north. But much of an ice age’s cold came from carbon dioxide leaving the air. That carbon went into the ocean largely at the other end of the planet, around Antarctica.

A upcoming modeling study suggests the two ends were connected. Cooling only the ocean’s far north pulled nearly three-quarters as much CO2 out of the air as cooling the entire planet.

Madison Shankle of the University of St Andrews led the work with colleagues at the National Oceanography Centre and the University of Chicago.

The test ran in a simplified computer model of the ocean with no real ice sheet in it. So the result is a mechanism, not a measurement of the past.

Shankle stated the team had “produced evidence of a plausible mechanism” linking the northern ice sheets to the changes around Antarctica that pulled CO2 from the air.

“Our study takes the step of actually demonstrating them working in model simulations, which is a big step forward for this field,” Shankle added.

According to recent reports, ice ages are paced by slow wobbles in Earth’s orbit, which change how much summer sunlight reaches the far north. Less summer sun lets ice sheets grow there.

In a recent development, however, the wobbles alone can’t make the planet as cold as it got. And the deep ocean is the only store substantial enough to hold the missing carbon.

Recent findings suggest that much of the deep ocean’s water last touched the air in the Southern Ocean around Antarctica. This is where scientists have looked for the carbon.

Antarctic ice cores show that sea ice there grew and shrank in step with the northern ice sheets,. It did not change with the sunlight over Antarctica itself.

Recent findings suggest that in 2001, two researchers proposed an answer. Cold water sinks in the North Atlantic and flows south through the deep ocean.

Industry observers note that if a northern ice sheet chilled that water, the chill would eventually arrive around Antarctica. This would cause sea ice to grow there, and set off the changes that store carbon.

It has been revealed that shankle’s team tested the idea in the MITgcm ocean model. The model ocean is one basin, 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) deep. It has a flat floor and runs from 70 degrees south to 70 degrees north.

Recent findings suggest that air temperatures over it are fixed, so it can’t grow an ice sheet,. The team cooled the air to stand in for one.

It has been revealed that the team ran four versions. One had warm, preindustrial-style air everywhere, and one was ice-age cold everywhere, 3.6°F (2°C) cooler at the equator and 10.8°F (6°C) cooler at the poles.

The other two cooled only the air north of 40.5 degrees north, either halfway to ice-age temperatures or all the way.

The cooled band is where northern water sinks to the deep, and it is small. It covers just 13 percent of the model’s surface. Each run lasted 15,000 model years, long enough for the deep ocean to settle.

Cooling the north cooled the whole model ocean. The biggest temperature drop was at mid-depths of 3,300 to 6,600 feet (1,000 to 2,000 meters). In the fully cooled northern run, that layer ended up colder than under global cooling.

In a recent development, the far north turned out to have outsized reach. In the full northern run, the whole ocean cooled by 4.5°F (2.5°C) on average. An earlier run that applied the same cooling to the far south instead cooled the whole ocean by only 1.1°F (0.6°C).

The cold water grew sea ice around the model’s Antarctica, and ice thickness south of 60 degrees south roughly doubled in the half-cooled run and tripled in the full one.

Sources indicate that thicker ice leaves more salt behind when it freezes, so the bottom water got saltier and the deep ocean separated into more distinct layers. Records of the real ice ages show both features.

Atmospheric CO2 in the model fell by 14 parts per million with the half-cooled north, and 32 ppm with the fully cooled one. Cooling the whole planet brought it down 43 ppm. So the north alone produced 74 percent of the drawdown.

Most of that came from a simple fact: cold water holds more carbon dioxide.

Because the northern cooling reached the whole deep ocean, the extra carbon that the colder water absorbed matched or exceeded the global-cooling run.

The thicker Antarctic sea ice added more by capping water before it could give its carbon back to the air, at about half the strength of the global run.

Marine life worked against the storage: the cooler, more layered ocean left more nutrients unused at the surface, which released some carbon rather than storing it.

The real ice ages had iron-rich dust and shifting winds that fed ocean life, and the model has neither.

Air trapped in ice cores demonstrates CO2 fell from about 280 ppm to about 180 ppm, and the model wasn’t built to match that.

A 2022 study cooled the North Atlantic in a more realistic two-basin model and saw CO2 rise by 6 ppm instead. Its Atlantic current strengthened and brought deep carbon back toward the surface.

According to recent reports, in that model, the deep water started out warmer, about 43°F to 46°F (6°C to 8°C) against 36°F to 39°F (2°C to 4°C) in the upcoming one. It may not have cooled enough to grow southern sea ice, Shankle’s team wrote.

The new model has limits of its own. It has a flat floor, no real ice sheet, no changing winds, and no seasons, and its CO2 doesn’t warm or cool the air.

The air over its Antarctica also stayed at warm, preindustrial temperatures, which probably held back the sea ice and understated the effect, the authors wrote.

According to recent reports, whether a real ice sheet, with its winds and seasons, could set off the same chain in the real Southern Ocean is the open question. The team’s next step is a model with a growing ice sheet built in, and they want the idea tested in fuller models of the Earth.

The full study was published in the Journal of Climate.

Breaking: Spring hunting season seems to cause wild turkeys to hatch mostly female chicks, putting them at risk of extinction

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A turkey is the centerpiece of the Thanksgiving table, but for a wild male turkey, the riskiest time of year is spring.
  • According to recent reports, A turkey is the centerpiece of the Thanksgiving table, but for a wild male turkey, the riskiest time of year is spring.
  • Recent findings suggest that in parts of Georgia and Louisiana where the males were hunted, wild turkey hens hatched about two daughters for every son.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A turkey is the centerpiece of the Thanksgiving table, but for a wild male turkey, the riskiest time of year is spring. That’s when the birds breed, and….

According to recent reports, A turkey is the centerpiece of the Thanksgiving table, but for a wild male turkey, the riskiest time of year is spring. That’s when the birds breed, and it’s when hunters go after the males.

Recent findings suggest that in parts of Georgia and Louisiana where the males were hunted, wild turkey hens hatched about two daughters for every son. At a South Carolina site where the birds weren’t hunted, hens hatched sons and daughters in nearly equal numbers.

Recent findings suggest that the finding, from a study of turkey nests, suggests that spring hunting may do more than kill adult males. Hunting may also affect how many sons and daughters hatch.

In a recent development, erin Ulrey of the University of Georgia’s Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources was the study’s lead author. Ulrey’s team had predicted the opposite: more sons than daughters.

Recent findings suggest that the team compared three sites with turkey hunting to just one site without it. That comparison can show a pattern. It can’t prove hunting is the cause.

In an earlier study, researchers from the same school tracked 109 male turkeys during the hunting season to see which ones were killed by hunters or predators.

Ulrey’s team started by catching wild turkey hens in all three states between 2020 and 2023, using nets baited with cracked corn. They fitted each hen with a GPS tracker and let her go.

When a tracker showed a hen staying close to one spot for several days, the team knew she was nesting.

In a recent development, the researchers kept their distance. They checked on each nesting hen daily from more than 65 feet (20 meters) away, using the radio signal from her tracker.

After the eggs hatched, the researchers collected the empty shells. The thin lining inside an eggshell contains the chick’s DNA. A lab tested each lining for a version of a gene that only female birds have.

According to recent reports, the lab couldn’t read the DNA from every shell. In the end, the team knew the sex of 724 chicks from 83 nests. Of those chicks, 446 were daughters and 278 were sons.

Sources indicate that three of the four study sites were open to spring turkey hunting, one in Georgia and two in Louisiana. On those three sites, 285 of the 422 chicks were female, about two-thirds.

According to recent reports, the fourth site was the Savannah River Site, a U.S. Department of Energy property in South Carolina. The birds the team caught there weren’t hunted.

In a recent development, the only turkey hunts on the property during the study were one-day events for 25 hunters with limited mobility, in 2022 and 2023. Those hunts took place away from where the team caught birds.

Hens on that site hatched 161 daughters and 141 sons. A gap that small could be due to chance.

Sources indicate that the researchers also checked other things that might matter, including a hen’s age, the date she started laying, and the number of eggs she laid. None of them was linked to the sex of her chicks.

With those things taken into account, the researchers estimated the chance that any one chick would be male. Their estimate was 26% on the sites with hunting and 49% on the site without it.

By that estimate, a son was about half as likely where males were hunted.

In birds, the chromosome that determines a chick’s sex comes from the mother. So a hen may be able to control the sex of her chicks, the authors wrote. Scientists don’t fully understand how.

Researchers have reported uneven numbers of sons and daughters in several other bird species. For the turkeys, Ulrey’s team offered two explanations, and both could be true.

The first explanation is about which sex is more likely to breed. A daughter can breed in her first year. A son generally doesn’t start breeding until about age two.

Industry observers note that on the sites with hunting, hunters killed 29% of the adult males on average, and they usually killed the most birds in the first few weeks of the season. Some of those males likely died before they could mate.

By that reasoning, a hen living where males are hunted may leave more descendants by hatching daughters.

“If a female is visiting a male over several days and he disappears, she has to move on and try to find another male. If the females are experiencing this over time, they might be aware male mortality is higher,” Ulrey remarked.

Sources indicate that the second explanation is stress. Hunting began just as hens started laying eggs. The hunting may have stressed the hens, and stressed hens may have higher levels of stress hormones.

In earlier studies of other birds, mothers with higher levels of those hormones tended to have more female chicks.

For the earlier study, Nickolas Gulotta of the Warnell School and three colleagues looked at which males died.

The team analyzed GPS records from 109 adult males that wore backpack-style trackers between 2014 and 2023. Of those birds, 59 lived in Georgia and 50 in South Carolina, all on land open to hunting.

From those records, the team worked out each bird’s habits. Those included how far he stayed from forest edges and open ground, and how fast he traveled. A forest edge is the strip where trees meet open land.

Each male tended to stick to his own habits from day to day.

During the year each bird was tracked, hunters killed 27 of the 109 males, and predators killed 17.

In both states, males that stayed closer to forest edges were more likely to be shot. Predators were more likely to kill them too.

Earlier studies that tracked turkey hunters by GPS help explain why. Hunters mostly use logging roads and gravel roads to find turkeys, and those roads are bordered by forest edges.

Bobcats and coyotes, two of the turkeys’ predators, travel and hunt along the same edges.

In a recent development, forest edges aside, hunters in the two states didn’t shoot the same kinds of birds. In Georgia, hunters were more likely to shoot the males that traveled faster.

In South Carolina, it was the reverse. Hunters there were more likely to shoot the males that traveled more slowly.

Predators in both states were more likely to kill the slower males.

So in Georgia, hunters were less likely to shoot a slower male, and predators were more likely to kill him.

“It’s kind of a catch-22 where if they can survive that hunting season, they’re most likely going to be fine,” Gulotta said.

“But at the same time, too, if they don’t travel that fast and are predictable, then they have the potential to be killed by a predator.”.

If hunters kill the birds that take more risks, he noted, the turkeys that are left could be harder to find and harder to hunt.

Industry observers note that turkeys would only become harder to hunt that way if the habits are inherited, meaning parents pass them to their chicks through genes. The study didn’t test that, and Gulotta’s team called for future studies to do it.

The tracked males also didn’t avoid open ground once hunting began. In both states, they stayed closer to open ground during the hunting season than before it. That’s likely because hens use open ground throughout the breeding season.

Ulrey’s study had just one site without hunting. Only one earlier study had looked at the sex of wild turkey chicks. It was done in a part of Texas with very little hunting, and it found slightly more sons than daughters.

Ulrey’s team didn’t report measuring stress hormones in the hens. So they couldn’t test the stress explanation.

In about half of the 83 nests, the lab couldn’t tell the sex of one chick. Even if all those chicks were male, daughters would still outnumber sons, the team calculated.

Recent findings suggest that over the past two decades, wildlife managers have seen wild turkey numbers drop across large areas where the birds live. If hens in hunted populations keep hatching mostly daughters, the authors wrote, that could eventually affect how those populations grow.

Knowing what part hunting plays in turkey breeding can help people manage the birds “in a sustainable way so that hunting can continue for years and years,” Ulrey noted.

The authors recommended that managers keep checking the sex of latest chicks. They also encouraged similar studies elsewhere, especially in places with different spring hunting rules.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Avian Biology. The earlier study of male turkeys was published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

#135533. In 1621, a letter described the first Thanksgiving: 90 men, three days, five deer, but not a word about turkey

In 1621, a letter described the first Thanksgiving: 90 men, three days, five deer, but not a word about turkey

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During what is know as the "first Thanksgiving," four colonists went fowling and killed enough birds for almost a week.
  • Sources indicate that the best-known description of the harvest celebration that Americans now call the first Thanksgiving comes from a few lines in one letter.
  • Recent findings suggest that the writer was Edward Winslow, one of the English colonists at Plymouth, according to the historian who edited his letter in 1865.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During what is know as the "first Thanksgiving," four colonists went fowling and killed enough birds for almost a week. Records show wild turkeys were plentiful that fall.

Sources indicate that the best-known description of the harvest celebration that Americans now call the first Thanksgiving comes from a few lines in one letter. It was written at Plymouth on December 11, 1621, and signed only “E. W.”.

Recent findings suggest that the writer was Edward Winslow, one of the English colonists at Plymouth, according to the historian who edited his letter in 1865. He was writing to a friend who was planning to join the colony, and the celebration takes up just a handful of sentences.

It has been revealed that those sentences mention a hunt for birds, a visit by Massasoit and “some ninetie men,” three days of feasting and five deer. They do not mention turkey, and they do not use the word “thanksgiving.”.

According to recent reports, winslow started with the farm report. The colonists had planted “some twentie Acres of Indian Corne” in the spring and sowed “some six Acres of Barly & Pease.”.

Following “the manner of the Indians,” he wrote, they fertilized the ground with fish, which were plentiful and easy to catch “at our doores.”.

The corn, a crop that Native farmers in the Americas had grown for thousands of years and that was domesticated more than once in different regions, did well.

The barley was “indifferent good.” The peas were “not worth the gathering,” because the sun had parched them in the blossom.

By then, the colonists had built seven dwelling houses and four buildings for the use of the settlement.

“[O]ur harvest being gotten in, our Governour sent foure men on fowling, that so we might after a more speciall manner reioyce together,” Winslow wrote, in the spelling of the time.

Those four men, he wrote, “in one day killed as much fowle, as with a little helpe beside, served the Tech giant almost a weeke.”.

Sources indicate that during that time, the colonists “exercised our Armes,” and many Native people came to the settlement. Among them was Massasoit, whom Winslow called “their greatest King,” with “some ninetie men, whom for three dayes we entertained and feasted.”.

Massasoit’s men also went hunting. “[T]hey went out and killed fiue Deere,” Winslow wrote, “which they brought to the Plantation and bestowed on our Governour, and vpon the Captaine, and others.”.

Winslow wrote “fowle,” a general word for birds. He did not say which kinds the four men shot.

Turkey could have been among them. Governor William Bradford, writing his history of the colony years later, described that same fall.

According to recent reports, “And now begane to come in store of foule, as winter aproached,” Bradford wrote. “And besids water foule, ther was great store of wild Turkies, of which they tooke many, besids venison, &c.”.

Recent findings suggest that so turkeys were plentiful around Plymouth that autumn, and the colonists hunted them. But Winslow’s account of the celebration never names them.

Winslow’s letter was published in London in 1622, in a short book about the Plymouth colony now known as Mourt’s Relation.

It has been revealed that the letter also spoke to people thinking of making the voyage. “[A]lthough it be not alwayes so plentifull, as it was at this time with vs,” Winslow wrote, “yet by the goodnesse of God, we are so farre from want, that we often wish you partakers of our plentie.”.

Sources indicate that he ended with practical advice for his friend’s journey. Among other things, he told him to bring paper and linseed oil for the windows, and he advised, “let your shott be most for bigge Fowles.”.

Bradford later wrote that the plenty of that fall “made many afterwards write so largly of their plenty hear to their freinds in England, which were not fained, but true reports.”.

Winslow’s passage about the celebration does not call it a thanksgiving or present it as the start of a tradition.

Paintings like the one by Jean Leon Gerome Ferris, made around 1912 to 1915, show tables, costumes and feathered headdresses that appear nowhere in Winslow’s few lines.

What the letter does preserve is simpler: a good corn harvest, a bird hunt, a three-day visit, and five deer brought in by Massasoit’s men. Turkeys have a much longer history in North America than that meal. Scientists have found that turkeys were domesticated at least 1,500 years ago.

The information was obtained from Edward Winslow’s letter of December 11, 1621, published in A Relation or Iournall of the beginning and proceedings of the English Plantation setled at Plimoth in Fresh England (London, 1622; Boston Public Library copy), and from William Bradford’s History “Of Plimoth Plantation”, printed by order of the General Court of Massachusetts in 1899.

An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • In a recent development, in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • Sources indicate that what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

Sources indicate that what is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

In a recent development, californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

In a recent development, state officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

According to recent reports, in 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she claims. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this new climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

In a recent development, in 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Sources indicate that not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” indicates Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

In a recent development, but there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto indicates. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, claims Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

It has been revealed that the El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

Sources indicate that as much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

Sources indicate that “We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves noted. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

In a recent development, the neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves says. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

In a recent development, gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

He reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves notes.

Industry observers note that the havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier indicates. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk matter,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report noted.

California’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier notes. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

Such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a big boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Recent findings suggest that months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, states Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

According to recent reports, as prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Industry observers note that those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, says she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she says. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

But, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.

Industry News: No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, senate Democratic leader Charles E.
  • Industry observers note that ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said.
  • Industry observers note that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, Upcoming Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”.

Industry observers note that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Sources indicate that now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A significant takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ latest populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

Sources indicate that white evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

Sources indicate that if you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

It has been revealed that if one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

Washing your Thanksgiving turkey spreads germs around the kitchen, but a USDA study highlights skipping it is also a bad idea

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Washing a Thanksgiving turkey spreads germs, the USDA says.
  • According to recent reports, many families rinse the Thanksgiving turkey in the kitchen sink before it goes in the oven, because that is how a parent or grandparent always did it.
  • According to recent reports, “USDA research has found that washing or rinsing meat or poultry increases the risk for cross-contamination in the kitchen,” the agency’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Washing a Thanksgiving turkey spreads germs, the USDA says. But its 2019 test-kitchen study found the sink and poorly washed hands mattered more than splashes.

According to recent reports, many families rinse the Thanksgiving turkey in the kitchen sink before it goes in the oven, because that is how a parent or grandparent always did it. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) has been telling people for years to stop.

According to recent reports, “USDA research has found that washing or rinsing meat or poultry increases the risk for cross-contamination in the kitchen,” the agency’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) states. Cooking the bird to the right temperature kills the germs, so washing it is “risky and not necessary for safety.”.

The research behind that advice holds a twist, though. The agency’s key experiment did not use turkeys.

According to recent reports, when USDA-funded scientists filmed 300 home cooks preparing chicken thighs in test kitchens, many of the people who skipped washing their chicken still ended up with its bacteria in their salads. Their sinks and their hands spread it anyway.

According to recent reports, the study was carried out for FSIS by RTI International and North Carolina State University (NCSU), and its final report was dated August 20, 2019. It was the second round of a five-year FSIS consumer food safety research project.

Industry observers note that the team set up eight test kitchens in the Raleigh-Durham area and in Lillington, a rural town in North Carolina. Every participant had said they wash or rinse raw poultry when cooking at home.

Sources indicate that before their appointments, 142 of them received three emails with USDA food safety messages. One remarked not to wash poultry and linked to a USDA video; one recommended separate cutting boards for raw meat and ready-to-eat food; and one was a USDA “Clean” infographic about not washing poultry and about washing hands and kitchen surfaces.

The other 158 participants received nothing.

In the kitchen, six cameras recorded every move. Each person cooked chicken thighs and made a mixed green salad.

What they did not know was that the chicken had been spiked with a harmless, traceable strain of E. coli called DH-5 alpha.

After the meal and the cleanup, the researchers swabbed the kitchen surfaces, tested the lettuce and counted where the marker bacteria had ended up.

In a recent development, the messages changed what people did with the chicken. In the group that got the emails, 93% did not wash the chicken, compared with 39% in the group that did not.

In a recent development, those who did wash it mostly rinsed it in the sink rather than submerging it. Asked why they wash chicken at home, 30% said they wanted to remove blood or slime, and 19% said it was how a family member did it.

Two-thirds of the participants who got the emails, 66%, said the messages had changed how they cooked that day.

Then came the lab results. Lettuce from the salads carried the marker bacteria in 26% of the cooks who had washed their chicken and in 20% of those who had not. Washing made things somewhat worse, but skipping it was far from a fix.

Sources indicate that the researchers suspect hands were an crucial factor. Handwashing was covered in one of the emails, but it did not change how participants washed their hands.

In a recent development, of all the handwashing that should have happened before or during the meal, only 2% included every step the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends. The most common mistake was not rubbing hands with soap for at least 20 seconds.

Sources indicate that the report also found high levels of the marker in the sink. Microbes that reach the sink from the chicken, its packaging or contaminated hands “are a larger cause for concern than splashing contaminated chicken fluids onto the counter,” the authors wrote.

A sink that is not cleaned properly can pass germs to whatever is rinsed in it next, such as lettuce or vegetables. Researchers have warned before that the sink deserves as much attention as your hands.

When the study was published in the Journal of Food Protection in 2022, Ellen Shumaker, its corresponding author at NC State, summed it up.

“Washing the chicken is still not a good idea, but this study demonstrates the need to focus on preventing contamination of sinks and emphasizing the importance of hand-washing and cleaning and sanitizing surfaces,” she remarked.

Another finding: only 47% of all participants used a food thermometer on at least one chicken thigh.

In a release on November 13, the USDA reminded families that a food thermometer is the only way to know a turkey is done.

Recent findings suggest that the bird is safe at 165°F, checked in three places: the thickest part of the breast, the innermost part of the wing and the innermost part of the thigh. Stuffing is best cooked separately, and if it goes inside the turkey, its center must also reach 165°F.

Industry observers note that for a frozen turkey, the agency indicates never to thaw it on the counter. In the refrigerator, allow about 24 hours for every 4 to 5 pounds.

In cold water, allow about 30 minutes per pound and change the water every 30 minutes. A fresh turkey should be bought one to two days before cooking.

Washing raw meat or poultry is not recommended, according to FSIS, and soap or detergent should never be used on it. Rinsing in salt water, vinegar or lemon juice does not make it safer either.

Kitchen surfaces should be cleaned first with hot, soapy water and then sanitized. Germs can linger: Campylobacter can survive in a kitchen for up to 4 hours and Salmonella for up to 32 hours, the agency indicates.

Sources indicate that leftovers should go in the refrigerator within two hours. They keep for up to four days and should be reheated to 165°F.

Every year, USDA food safety specialists answer thousands of Thanksgiving questions through the agency’s Meat and Poultry Hotline. It is normally open Monday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern Time.

On Thanksgiving Day, November 26, 2026, it will be open from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Eastern Time at 1-888-MPHotline (1-888-674-6854). Questions can also be sent by email to MPHotline@usda.gov.

Food is not the only holiday hazard in the house: earth.com has also looked at which Thanksgiving leftovers are safe to give your dog.

The information was obtained from the USDA’s November 13, 2026, Thanksgiving food safety release, the FSIS post From Freezer to Feast, the FSIS page Washing Food: Does it Promote Food Safety?, the 2019 final report of the poultry washing experiment and NC State’s 2022 release on the published study.

Seabirds named George and Geraldine returned for their 10th anniversary as a couple

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Short-tailed albatrosses George and Geraldine returned to Midway Atoll for their 10th year together, offering hope for this endangered species.
  • Two short-tailed albatrosses known as George and Geraldine are back on Sand Island at Midway Atoll, which lies in the North Pacific.
  • Their arrival was confirmed in late October 2026, marking the 10th straight year the two have returned as a pair, according to the Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Short-tailed albatrosses George and Geraldine returned to Midway Atoll for their 10th year together, offering hope for this endangered species.

Two short-tailed albatrosses known as George and Geraldine are back on Sand Island at Midway Atoll, which lies in the North Pacific.

Their arrival was confirmed in late October 2026, marking the 10th straight year the two have returned as a pair, according to the Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP).

Recent findings suggest that ACAP describes them as the only short-tailed albatrosses breeding in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Together they have raised and fledged at least five chicks.

According to recent reports, both birds were banded as chicks on Japan’s Torishima island. George hatched there in 2003 and has visited Midway since November 2006, when he was known as “Lonesome George.”.

Geraldine is thought to be a bird banded on Torishima in April 2008. She was first seen on Midway in early 2012, ACAP reported in 2024.

The two were first seen together in late 2016 and first shared a nest the following season.

That 2017/18 season, they incubated an egg laid by a black-footed albatross, and the chick fledged. Black-footed and Laysan albatrosses also nest on Sand Island.

Geraldine’s sex was still listed as unconfirmed in 2018. She settled the question by laying the egg the two incubated in October 2023.

Before them, another short-tailed pair raised chicks on Midway’s Eastern Island, most recently in 2013/14. Its male was found dead there in November 2014.

It has been revealed that george and Geraldine’s own first chick hatched on Jan. 3, 2019, and biologists banded it that May. It left its nest site earlier than expected, in late May, and became the first chick known to fledge from Sand Island.

Short-tailed albatross chicks hatch from late December through January, and each breeding cycle lasts about eight months.

It has been revealed that their next chick left in 2020. It walked across Sand Island before taking off over the water, likely to spend five or more years at sea.

“Nature has a way of reminding us that species and populations often have a remarkable capacity for resilience and fuel our hopes for recovering natural systems,” said Jonathan Plissner, then an island restoration specialist at Island Conservation, in 2020.

Not every season has worked. The 2021/22 egg did not hatch.

Sources indicate that A chick that fledged in 2022/23 returned in April 2024 and displayed with one hatched in 2019/20. That November, two of their earlier chicks were photographed within a few feet of Geraldine as she incubated.

Sources indicate that in late 2024, a fifth short-tailed albatross was also on Sand Island. The sub-adult, nicknamed Forest Bird, came from the same Torishima cohort as Geraldine and lived alone about a mile (1.6 kilometers) from the others.

Sources indicate that george and Geraldine had no success in 2024/25. They bred again in 2025/26, when eight different short-tailed albatrosses were recorded on the atoll, three of them their offspring.

Those returning young birds may eventually start breeding on Midway themselves.

In a recent development, in Hawaiian, the short-tailed albatross is called makalena. Around the turn of the 20th century, feather hunters killed millions of them, nearly wiping out the species, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS).

The agency listed the species as endangered throughout its range in 2000. A 2020 review estimated the population at 7,365 birds, growing about 8.9 percent a year.

It is the largest albatross in the North Pacific, with wings spanning about 7 to 7.5 feet (213 to 229 centimeters).

Short-tailed albatrosses begin breeding at five or six years old. Parents take turns on the egg and alternate foraging trips that can last two to three weeks.

Recent findings suggest that torishima, the main colony, is an active volcano. In 2010, a landslide there buried up to ten chicks.

Between 2008 and 2012, chicks moved from Torishima to Mukojima started a third colony.

Sources indicate that these albatrosses spend most of their lives at sea, ranging from China and Japan to Russia, Alaska and Canada. The highest concentrations occur around the Aleutian Islands and in the Bering Sea.

Industry observers note that birds that follow fishing boats can be hooked or tangled in longline gear and drown. Albatross chicks can also choke and die after eating plastic.

On land, Midway brings its own threat. Mice were first seen attacking albatrosses on the atoll in December 2015.

The Midway Seabird Protection Project spread bait across Sand Island by helicopter on July 20 and 21, 2023. Crews also scattered bait by hand in sensitive areas and used bait boxes around buildings.

By Aug. 15, mice were still being found, and eradication efforts were stopped.

The project then moved into what the USFWS calls a “Mitigation and Learning Phase.” A similar attempt on Gough Island also failed to remove mice that attack albatrosses and other seabirds.

The information was obtained from the Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels.
