💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Maya people had a toxic relationship with the color red—quite literally, according to fresh research.
  • According to recent reports, “The mercury data was crazy,” Matt Waters, an environmental sciences professor and paleolimnologist at Auburn University, said in a university statement about the unexpected discovery on the peninsula.
  • Matt Waters led a study published in Science Advances that explored sediment samples collected at two lakes—Lago Coba and Cenote Xcach—showing the intense spike in mercury (Hg) levels ranging from around 40 C.E.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Maya people had a toxic relationship with the color red—quite literally, according to fresh research. The latest analysis of the Yucatán Peninsula during the Maya era identified astronomically spiked levels of mercury, which might have contributed to the collapse of Maya culture.

According to recent reports, “The mercury data was crazy,” Matt Waters, an environmental sciences professor and paleolimnologist at Auburn University, said in a university statement about the unexpected discovery on the peninsula. “Off the charts. These mercury levels aren’t normal.”.

Matt Waters led a study published in Science Advances that explored sediment samples collected at two lakes—Lago Coba and Cenote Xcach—showing the intense spike in mercury (Hg) levels ranging from around 40 C.E. to 800 C.E.

“We show that Classic Period Hg concentrations in sediment cores from two lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula exceeded modern sediment Hg toxicity thresholds by orders of magnitude for centuries during ancient Maya occupation,” the authors wrote, adding that the heightened pollution coincides with aquatic food collapse, “confirming that Hg toxicity was an additional environmental stressor for Classic Maya populations.”.

While Waters isn’t saying mercury caused the collapse of the Maya civilization, he also doesn’t want to ignore its impact. “It’s been confirmed that drought was an issue, deforestation was an issue, erosion was an issue, overpopulation was an issue, and feeding the population was probably an issue,” he said. “This study adds the impact of water quality. Let’s put that in the list. That’s what our study does. It establishes that list and moves it forward.”.

It has been revealed that the study actually began as part of a National Science Foundation project focused on harmful algal blooms, but a then-graduate student and study co-author, Savanna Wooten, suggested also testing for heavy metals. Sediment coring from the lake bottoms pulled up mud from thousands of years ago that contained the intense mercury spikes during the Classic Maya Period, which were then followed by an abrupt decline.

The powerfully high mercury concentration lasted for hundreds of years, and Waters believes the sudden change at the base level likely moved up the food web, impacting fish and other larger creatures. Not only would eating fish or drinking water have exposed humans to the toxic levels, but there may have even been fewer fish to catch. “They would have seen a strange color change in the water,” Waters told Live Science, “and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein.”.

Waters linked to a study he’d worked on with a team from the University of Florida in the late 1990s that found a gap in ostracod shells during a specific period from Coba, correlating the missing shell timing to the rise in mercury. Further investigation into the cores found that declines in biological markers occurred throughout. “The algae was killed,” he noted. “The cyanobacteria, they tanked. Purple sulfur bacteria, vanished. The biological community completely changed.”.

The people “experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries.”.

The source of that mercury was cinnabar, they believe, a vibrant red mineral made up of 86 percent mercury that Maya culture viewed as a sacred pigment. “This was not like mercury raining down from the sky,” Waters said. “This was not a regional thing. It was concentrated.”.

Maya loved cinnabar, using the bright red in pottery, murals, temple walls, and burials. To keep up with demand, they heavily imported it, especially around Coba and Xcach. “It’s common knowledge that there was trade in obsidian, in jade, and beautiful stones, and weaponry,” Waters said. “I think this could start a conversation that cinnabar could have been a major trade commodity.”.

It may also show a highly toxic love affair that contributed to Maya struggles.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#135525. Tech Report: How cranberries went from a Thanksgiving favorite to a symbol of stronger farming for the future

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1112 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: How cranberries went from a Thanksgiving favorite to a symbol of stronger farming for the future

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Breeding cultivated cranberries with wild relatives may help protect future crops from extreme heat, frost and climate change.
  • Cranberries grow in some of the coldest parts of North America, but frost can still damage them.
  • In a recent development, in spring, frost can damage newly growing buds before they produce berries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Breeding cultivated cranberries with wild relatives may help protect future crops from extreme heat, frost and climate change.

Cranberries grow in some of the coldest parts of North America, but frost can still damage them.

In a recent development, in spring, frost can damage newly growing buds before they produce berries. In early fall, it can harm fruit that is still ripening.

Scientists crossed cultivated cranberries with a small wild relative from the far north called Vaccinium oxycoccos.

When exposed to cold, these newly introduced plants kept more genes involved in growth active than cultivated cranberries did.

The wild plant’s DNA could therefore be of use in breeding cranberries that handle cold weather better.

Audrey Dickinson, a researcher in agricultural genomics at the San Diego Botanic Garden and the Salk Institute, led the study.

Scientists from the USDA’s Agricultural Research Service in Chatsworth, Latest Jersey, also took part.

Only leaves were sampled, over a span of minutes. Berries and harvests were not included.

According to recent reports, the United States is the world’s largest cranberry producer. Strawberries are the only berry Americans eat more of. Most cranberries reach shoppers as juice or as sweetened dried fruit.

In a recent development, berries can scald once the air passes about 90°F (32°C), and scalded fruit rots more easily. Frost, on the other hand, can leave the fruit soft.

When growers were surveyed, New Jersey producers named heat tolerance first. Wisconsin and British Columbia growers named frost tolerance.

In a recent development, one round of cranberry breeding takes seven to eight years. Most varieties are only a few generations away from wild vines. Wheat breeders, for one, have borrowed heat tolerance from wild relatives.

The small cranberry grows across the cold far north. As its name suggests, its berries are smaller than those of the farmed species.

The two plants look different, but they cross easily. Gene by gene, their published genomes line up closely.

According to recent reports, wild plants for this work were collected in southeastern Alaska in 1996. In 1998, four of them were crossed with the farmed varieties Stevens, Ben Lear and Pilgrim.

For three days, the team kept Stevens and the four hybrid lines at 70°F (21°C). Then the plants went into incubators.

The heated plants reached 117°F (47°C) in 30 minutes, while the chilled plants cooled to 37°F (3°C) over 95 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that the team clipped leaves three times and froze them in liquid nitrogen. Their RNA was read with Oxford Nanopore sequencing, which kept the wild and farmed gene copies apart.

Recent findings suggest that plants need proteins to grow. Ribosomes assemble those proteins, and the genes that build ribosomes are tied to growth.

Photosynthesis genes, used by leaves to turn sunlight into energy-rich sugars, are tied to growth as well.

Ribosome gene activity declined during the cold test in both Stevens and the hybrids, but the decline was greater in Stevens.

Photosynthesis gene activity increased in the hybrids but decreased in Stevens.

Basic cell work, the researchers suggested, kept going in the hybrids under stress. In Stevens, that work was reduced. Total photosynthesis gene activity, however, stayed higher in Stevens under every condition.

The two groups differed much more in cold than in heat. In the cold test, 18 broad sets of related genes behaved differently between hybrids and Stevens. In the heat test, only one set did.

The team linked this to where the parents come from. The farmed cranberry is native farther south. It may photosynthesize best at warmer temperatures.

A chill that stresses Stevens may be closer to normal growing weather for its wild Alaskan cousin.

The four hybrid lines did not respond in the same way. Gene activity differed more among the lines than between the hybrids as a group and Stevens.

Two lines with the same Stevens parent also differed from each other. The wild parents were therefore likely a major source of this variation.

In the cold test, two lines revealed an unusual pattern. At 60 minutes their gene activity shot up. By 95 minutes it had fallen, although the air was still getting colder. In Stevens, large changes continued to the end.

In a recent development, the team sees that rise and fall as a possible sign of efficient adjustment to cold. Results in the heat test were different.

After 30 minutes of heat, Stevens showed the smallest overall change of all the plants.

Some hybrids may cope with cold better than Stevens, then, yet cope with heat worse.

Industry observers note that heat and cold tolerance may need separate tests in breeding programs. Coping with one is no guarantee for the other.

At room temperature, the hybrids mostly took after Stevens. Some 57% of compared genes tracked the farmed parent, against 14% for the Alaskan one.

About 22% of genes were less active in the hybrids than in either parent, many of them tied to photosynthesis. A cold acclimation gene called WCOR413 was among them.

That could hint at hybrid weakness, a known risk when two separately evolved genomes are merged.

Recent findings suggest that chloroplasts may be part of the explanation. These green structures are where photosynthesis takes place. Many photosynthesis proteins are coded in the cell’s main DNA but work inside chloroplasts.

Sources indicate that chloroplasts also carry a small amount of their own DNA. The two sets of DNA must work together. A mismatch between them could disrupt photosynthesis genes.

To keep the two in step, the authors suggested crossing hybrids back to a farmed cranberry mother several times.

It has been revealed that the experiments were short. Only the first 30 minutes of heat and the first 95 minutes of cold were studied. Longer or repeated stress may produce different results.

Gene activity is also only a partial guide to which proteins a plant makes.

The two temperature experiments were also quite different. The heat was intense enough to potentially kill the plants, while the cold temperature was still within the range that cranberries normally experience outdoors.

Sources indicate that the researchers also did not measure plant survival, growth or berry production. It is still unclear whether a calmer gene response means a hardier plant.

For Dickinson, the study also highlights why protecting wild plants matters.

“These results highlight the importance of conserving crop wild relatives in their natural habitats and in collections,” she wrote.

Future research could test whether these gene patterns match real frost and heat tolerance in the field.

The study is published in the journal Plants, People, Planet.

Digital twins of cancer patients could help doctors find better treatments

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Digital twins of breast tumors could help doctors predict treatment responses and identify potentially effective alternative drugs.
  • Recent findings suggest that ask a chatbot-style AI which drug to give a cancer patient, and it may offer an answer without providing a transparent, scientifically grounded explanation.
  • In London, a team took the opposite route: a program built from logic rather than statistics, which a doctor can open up and read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Digital twins of breast tumors could help doctors predict treatment responses and identify potentially effective alternative drugs.

Recent findings suggest that ask a chatbot-style AI which drug to give a cancer patient, and it may offer an answer without providing a transparent, scientifically grounded explanation. That, the researchers mentioned, has left many doctors skeptical of such tools.

In London, a team took the opposite route: a program built from logic rather than statistics, which a doctor can open up and read.

Run on virtual copies of 31 real tumors, the program predicted whether a patient’s treatment would work 74% of the time.

For 12 of the 13 patients whose incomplete response the model correctly predicted, it identified at least one additional drug that might have helped.

Jasmin Fisher of the UCL Cancer Institute led the work, with Pedro Victori as first author and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute.

Every result is a simulation checked against records from a trial that has already ended, and the drugs it suggested were not tested in the patients it picked them for.

“We see our computer model as an aid for existing cancer clinical practice, not an alternative to it,” Fisher remarked.

The cancer in question is triple-negative breast cancer, about 15% of breast cancers.

It has been revealed that its cells lack the three receptors that most breast cancer drugs aim at, so hormone therapies don’t work. About 40% of patients die within five years of diagnosis.

Sources indicate that instead of training on patient data, the team hand-built a map of how the disease works. They read 191 research papers and drew 142 genes, proteins and cell processes as nodes.

Then they linked the nodes with 379 arrows that say which one switches which on or off, and let each node be off, low or fully on.

Industry observers note that the map includes the machinery that repairs broken DNA, which chemotherapy and the drug olaparib attack. It also includes the machinery of cell division, which the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel jams.

Two output nodes sum it up: whether the cancer cells die, and whether they keep multiplying.

Before applying the model to individual tumors, the team checked it against 160 laboratory results from 33 other papers and adjusted it until it reproduced all of them.

According to recent reports, the patients came from PARTNER, a trial run by Jean Abraham’s team in Cambridge. Its patients, all with triple-negative breast cancer, received four chemotherapy drugs before surgery, with or without olaparib.

For 31 of them, the team had full genome sequences of the tumor.

Each patient’s mutations and missing or duplicated genes were loaded into the map to make a digital twin of the tumor.

A patient with a disabled BRCA1 gene, for instance, had that node fixed at zero. Then the twin was given the same treatment the patient had received, and the program reported whether the cells died.

Sources indicate that the predictions matched the real outcomes in 23 of 31 cases. The program was right for 10 of the 14 patients whose cancer disappeared completely, and for 13 of the 17 whose cancer did not.

Only those 23 accurate twins were used for what came next.

Industry observers note that the team then took the 13 twins that resisted treatment and switched off every gene in the map, one at a time. They watched for the switch that tipped the simulated cells into dying.

Twelve of the 13 had one. For 10, the program predicted a complete response, eight with a single added drug and two with a pair.

The most broadly useful target was a protein called ATM, which helps cells repair DNA damage; blocking it was predicted to produce a complete response in seven patients.

The other twins pointed to drugs that have passed phase 2 trials, including inhibitors of Chk1, ATR, MEK, mTOR and Wee1.

Fisher noted the point is to give a doctor a lead, not an order.

“In practice, the treatment option recommended by our model may, under closer scrutiny, be discounted by the clinician – for example, if they view the drug as too toxic,” she stated.

“But it may also lead them to explore, and eventually settle on, a third option which they might otherwise not have arrived at.”.

The one tumor for which the program could not identify an effective additional treatment contained three distinct populations of cancer cells.

Spatial RNA data demonstrated three groups of cells with different gene activity sitting in different parts of the tumor.

Simulated separately, each of the three had targets the whole-tumor model had missed. One of them, a lower-grade carcinoma, was predicted to respond completely to an added drug.

A sample taken after treatment held a fourth group unlike any of the first three, carrying two changes the model flags as resistance.

The team also pulled the 29 genes the program had flagged as targets and tested them as a signature in a public database of breast cancer patients.

Among patients with the basal subtype treated with chemotherapy alone, those carrying mutations in the signature genes lived longer.

Thirty-one patients is a small group, and the authors wrote that it limits how finely they can slice the results.

The model is right about three times in four, which also means it is wrong once in four. The twins that failed were set aside before the drug search began.

The map knows only what 191 papers told it, so it can’t propose a mechanism nobody has published.

It has been revealed that it also ignores the immune cells and other tissue around a tumor, which matter most for immunotherapy. And it models the drugs used in PARTNER rather than the newer antibody-drug conjugates now in use.

It has been revealed that each twin was built from DNA alone. The authors wrote that adding gene activity and protein data would likely sharpen the predictions.

The framework is designed to be updated as a patient’s tumor changes under treatment.

Determining whether the suggested drugs actually benefit patients will require a clinical trial in which the model’s predictions inform treatment decisions.

The full study was published in the journal Cell Reports Medicine.

The Government Tested How Dangerous AI Could Get—Then Four ChatBots Helped Plan a Terrorist Attack

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the dawn of artificial intelligence brings with it both rewards and risks.
  • Industry observers note that unfortunately, the risks of this technology are far from minuscule, including its impact on human education, the environment, and potentially the survival of the human race (an all-too-plausible scenario put forward by AI tech CEOs).
  • At least, that’s the latest conclusion by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan watchdog housed in the legislative branch of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the dawn of artificial intelligence brings with it both rewards and risks. With the ability to sift through unfathomably large data sets, AI could help detect cancers in their infancy, unlock some of the most enduring mysteries of mathematics, and even help contain the beating nuclear heart of future fusion reactors.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, the risks of this technology are far from minuscule, including its impact on human education, the environment, and potentially the survival of the human race (an all-too-plausible scenario put forward by AI tech CEOs). Even the everyday LLMs that now litter our digital lives—Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok—can aid and abet some of the most dangerous actors on the planet.

At least, that’s the latest conclusion by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan watchdog housed in the legislative branch of the U.S. government. Typically, GAO turns its investigative gaze on efforts to limit fraud and wasteful spending in the government itself, but in a upcoming tactic at the urging of U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH), the office instead performed real-world tests on the platform to see if these four popular AI models would aid in planning a terrorist attack.

Recent findings suggest that “A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Hassan, incoming Chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, remarked in a press statement. “Today’s newly introduced report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”.

GAO conducted this test in the spring this year, and earlier this week reported some disturbing results. Two of the platforms, according to an official GAO release, provided guidance on building and detonating an improvised explosion device, or IED, and two other AI models showing differing methods for targeting the electrical grid. Within 12 hours, all four models also gamed through potential locations and methods for carrying out such an attack.

Although these violent lines of questioning triggered each platform’s safeguards, GAO got around them using common safeguard-bypassing techniques. Additionally, they confirmed the validity of the information provided with experts. The results of this investigation were published in a 61-page report that will be central to future senate hearings on AI safety.

Sources indicate that “We set out to do two different types of evil,” GAO director Kevin Walsh noted in an interview posted on YouTube. “The first type is we wanted to create a bomb. And we didn’t just want to know how to create a bomb, we wanted it to help pick out a target, a location, and a time, and to give us instructions all the way…Evil scenario two, we wanted to do a bunch of economic damage, and in both cases that ended up being targeting the electrical grid.”.

In one case, Walsh reports that one AI model would refuse to answer questions or divert the user to more safe behaviors but mentioned that “it wasn’t always successful.” Walsh notes that companies theoretically call law enforcement when suspicious activity is detected, but whether that occurs and at what frequency is uncertain.

“As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the report concludes. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.”.

The GAO officially released these terrorist-abetting findings on November 18, 2026, the same day Anthropic, creators of Claude, went public on the stock exchange. Despite the company’s own admission of AI being an existential threat to humanity, its IPO at one point reached a meteoric a $2 trillion valuation before dipping back down to a (measly) $1.6 trillion.

Sources indicate that darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

Putting down your phone may have less to do with willpower than you think

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1612 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Problematic internet use may affect over 10% of people worldwide, prompting experts to call for safer digital platforms.
  • You pick up your phone to answer one message.
  • That lost hour is usually put down to poor willpower.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Problematic internet use may affect over 10% of people worldwide, prompting experts to call for safer digital platforms.

You pick up your phone to answer one message. An hour later, you’re still scrolling through videos you never meant to watch.

That lost hour is usually put down to poor willpower. A report from an international panel of experts treats it instead as a global public health concern.

According to their estimate, problematic internet use may affect more than 10% of people worldwide.

Part of the blame, the authors argue, lies with the way apps and websites are designed by technology companies.

The report comes from the Lancet Psychiatry Commission on global action on problematic usage of the internet.

Psychiatrists, psychologists and public health researchers from several countries began the work in February 2023.

It has been revealed that people who had struggled with their own internet use were involved from the start. They served as advisers throughout the project.

No upcoming experiment was run. Instead, the commission reviewed existing studies and turned the findings into recommendations for governments.

Some online habits are already recognized as medical conditions. Gaming disorder and gambling disorder both appear in the World Health Organization’s ICD-11 classification.

Compulsive social media use and problem online shopping haven’t received that status yet.

It has been revealed that then there’s cyberchondria. That’s when someone keeps searching their symptoms online and grows more anxious with every search.

Recent findings suggest that not everyone who spends hours online has a disorder. The researchers describe a spectrum, running from useful, productive time online to habits that seriously disrupt daily life.

Zsolt Demetrovics is a professor of psychology at ELTE Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest and at Flinders University in Australia.

He sat on the commission’s four-member steering group, which was chaired by Naomi Fineberg of the University of Hertfordshire.

“Digital technologies are now woven into almost every aspect of modern life and bring enormous benefits,” Demetrovics said.

The commission isn’t trying to get people offline. Its focus is on stopping everyday use from turning harmful.

Internet use is now reported by an estimated 6 billion people, or roughly three-quarters of the world’s total population.

Social media platforms are used for an average of 3.5 hours per day by people aged 16 to 24.

Rates of problematic use above 10% have often been reported in meta-analyses that included pandemic-era studies.

A prevalence of around 7% had been estimated for the period before the COVID-19 pandemic.

It has been revealed that estimates vary depending on how researchers define and measure problematic internet use. One pandemic-era study put the figure at 25%, but stricter criteria brought it down to 7.9%.

Researchers still cannot say whether the problem is growing worldwide. Even the lowest estimates, however, represent millions of people.

Studies suggest that gaming disorder affects 2% to 12% of people. Around 5% struggle with social media use, while 16% struggle with compulsive online shopping.

Problems with gambling, gaming and pornography are more common among males.

Females more often struggle with social media, online shopping and cyberchondria.

Higher rates have also been reported in low-income and middle-income countries than in wealthier ones.

It has been revealed that young people seem especially vulnerable. Brain changes during the teenage years can make it harder to control impulses, which may be part of the reason.

In a recent development, think about what happens when a video ends. Another one starts on its own, and there’s always something else waiting.

Features such as infinite scroll, autoplay and personalized recommendations can make it hard to stop.

The commission also flagged unpredictable rewards, gambling-like features, pop-ups and tools that invite people to compare themselves with others.

Andrea Czakó, a senior research fellow in psychology at Flinders University, was one of the report’s authors.

“Many digital products are intentionally designed to capture and hold our attention,” Czakó mentioned.

The ever-increasing power of artificial intelligence to strengthen such designs and algorithms was flagged as a further concern.

The effects of AI chatbots on young people were described by the authors as barely investigated.

Most gambling and gaming and social media platforms are owned by a relatively small number of transnational corporations.

Ownership by a handful of gatekeeper firms was seen by the commission as both a challenge and an opportunity.

Industry observers note that powerful technology companies have tended to resist regulation. Natural checkpoints in the market could nonetheless be required to help enforce international standards.

A similar argument about design and young people was made in a recent Lancet series on digital media.

Problematic internet use frequently co-occurs with ADHD, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbances and eating disorders.

It has been revealed that but which problem comes first? Most studies examined people at a single point in time, making it difficult to determine which problem came first.

In gambling disorder, however, other mental disorders were found to precede the gambling problem in about 75% of instances.

Less evidence exists for the direction of such relationships in other forms of problematic internet use.

Some longitudinal studies have linked online social activity in young people to subsequent ADHD symptoms, but not the reverse.

Poor sleep may help explain why problem social media use is linked to depression and anxiety.

Separate research has tied screen use in bed to a higher risk of insomnia among young adults.

It has been revealed that in the commission’s view, these problems can feed each other. Low mood may push someone online, and heavy use may then make things worse.

In a recent development, how much does problematic internet use cost society? Few estimates of the economic costs or societal burdens were found to exist.

A worked example for the UK was therefore produced by the commission using a prevalence-based cost-of-illness approach.

A base case of about 5% prevalence and around 3.3 million affected individuals was assumed for this example.

The total annual economic cost of problematic use in the UK was conservatively put at approximately £10 to £12 billion.

That amount corresponds to about 0.4% of UK gross domestic product.

About half of the total was found to come from hard-to-see losses such as foregone productivity and quality-of-life decrements.

Most of the burden of problematic internet use was therefore judged to fall outside traditional health-care spending.

The precise figures were acknowledged to be open to debate by the authors of the model.

Gaming disorder had been estimated in one earlier study to cost South Korea approximately $3.5 billion per year.

The commission surveyed addiction societies in 38 countries across Europe, Asia, Oceania, the Americas and Africa.

In 31 of them, treatments such as cognitive behavioral therapy were available. This therapy helps people notice and change unhelpful patterns of thinking and behavior.

Yet 30 of the 38 societies mentioned a lack of professional certification was a major gap.

Cognitive behavioral therapy has the strongest evidence so far, especially when it’s delivered in groups.

Still, few clinical trials have tested treatments for problematic internet use, and their quality is often low.

Regulatory frameworks have been used with success within similar areas of public health and safety such as alcohol and gambling.

A wide range of measures with potential for the regulation of problematic internet use was suggested on that basis.

Safety by design was described in the report as a key principle for regulating digital products and platforms.

Age restrictions and product disclosure of risks and harms and the enforcement of safety and quality standards were also recommended.

Recent findings suggest that australia was the first country to pass a law restricting social media access for children under 16. Platforms there must take reasonable steps to keep under-16s from holding accounts.

In the UK, the Age-Appropriate Design Code recommends limiting features such as autoplay and infinite scroll for children.

Industry observers note that in the US, the Surgeon General has called for warning labels on social media platforms. A separate trial has tested how teenagers respond to such warnings.

Countries including Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea and China have introduced restrictions on online gaming time.

The outcomes of these policies have been controversial and their effectiveness has been questioned in recent research.

Loot boxes, which hand out random rewards in video games, have been classified as gambling in Belgium. Enforcement of the resulting ban has been difficult.

Restrictive school smartphone policies might reduce smartphone usage during the school day according to recent UK data.

No significant difference in overall phone usage or mental wellbeing among young people was made by such policies.

Some projects are trying prevention instead of restriction.

A European project called BootStRaP recruits young people through schools and offers them flexible support through an app.

“The challenge is finding ways to reduce harms while preserving the many benefits of being connected,” Demetrovics stated.

Estimates of prevalence were acknowledged to vary substantially according to the definitions and assessment instruments and thresholds and regions used.

Recent findings suggest that proxy variables such as screen time have been used even in high-quality studies. Screen time is not equivalent to problematic use.

The effectiveness of many of the regulatory policies described in the report is yet to be fully evaluated.

The existing evidence base was nonetheless considered sufficient by the commission to justify immediate national and internationally coordinated action.

Large-scale longitudinal studies with standardised assessment were called for to clarify the course and outcomes of problematic use.

Future research could test whether restricting engagement features such as autoplay and infinite scroll reduces problematic internet use.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet Psychiatry.

#135520. Industry News: Donkeys help families survive droughts, but governments often overlook them

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1494 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Donkeys help families survive droughts, but governments often overlook them

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1494 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Donkeys help East African families survive severe droughts, yet governments and aid organizations often overlook their essential needs.
  • Families in East Africa depend on donkeys for many everyday tasks.
  • According to recent reports, in a drought their job gets even more important.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Donkeys help East African families survive severe droughts, yet governments and aid organizations often overlook their essential needs.

Families in East Africa depend on donkeys for many everyday tasks. The animals carry water, feed for livestock, and household belongings. They have also been part of local culture for generations.

According to recent reports, in a drought their job gets even more important. Once the water close to home has dried up, donkeys trek long distances to bring it back.

Industry observers note that yet when drought relief arrives, donkeys are rarely part of it. Aid has tended to go to the food-producing animals, and donkey-owning households end up worse off for it.

A team from the University of Portsmouth, Maasai Mara University and Haramaya University looked at how far that neglect goes.

They went through 77 documents and talked with 41 people on the ground. Donkeys, it turned out, are mostly missing, from the policies right down to the vet schools.

Industry observers note that from 2020 to 2023 East Africa was hit by drought. Crops failed widely and some places lost up to 70% of livestock.

Around 26 million people were threatened with food shortages, and conflict over the dwindling resources went up.

Many of the worst affected families are pastoralists, meaning their living depends on herds that often move with them.

Donkeys have been part of that life since they were domesticated in Africa thousands of years ago.

Recent findings suggest that when nearby sources dry up, the water a donkey brings back keeps people, crops and herds going. Donkeys also get people to health facilities, aid distribution centers and markets.

Recent findings suggest that kenya and Ethiopia both rely heavily on them. Ethiopia has about 10.8 million donkeys, and Kenya around 1.2 million.

Professor Leanne Proops works on animal behavior and welfare at the University of Portsmouth and supervised the project.

“Working donkeys are a lifeline for many communities during drought, helping people access water, transport essential supplies and sustain their livelihoods,” said Proops.

“Yet their contribution is largely overlooked in the policies and support systems designed to help communities cope with these crises.”.

Of the 77 documents, 51 were Kenyan and 26 Ethiopian, issued anywhere from 1964 up to 2025.

It has been revealed that animal health, agriculture, climate change, disaster risk and water were the areas covered. Equids, that is donkeys, horses and mules, came up in just 17.

Quite often the donkey got one mention in a species list and was absent from the rest of the policy.

“Livestock” was a word used a lot, but most documents never remarked what species it took in. In reality it meant cattle, sheep and goats.

Donkeys, on the occasions they did appear, sat outside conventional livestock under labels such as “working animals” or “emerging livestock.”.

Not one of the documents made a link between donkeys and drought, even though camels were mentioned in that role.

According to recent reports, on welfare the picture is not much better. Kenya’s Animal Welfare and Protection Bill has been in deliberation since 2019 without being enacted.

Up until 2025, Ethiopia’s criminal code only made cruelty an offense when it happened where the public could see.

A 2025 proclamation now prohibits overloading or overworking any working animal, though no penalties are set out in that part.

Recent findings suggest that references to animals in the policies were heavily based on use, with meat, milk, hides and exports driving them. Kenya’s 2024 Livestock Bill does define donkeys as draught animals but welfare hardly features.

According to recent reports, the interviews pointed the same way. If a drought is forecast, preparedness plans kick in with worming and vaccination for the other livestock.

Recent findings suggest that “The donkeys were generally left out. Nobody was thinking about them,” one participant in Kenya told the researchers.

Later on, supplementary feed rations get handed out in both countries and again the donkeys are not counted.

A participant in Ethiopia noted that when fodder runs short, “the priority is not for donkeys, not for mules, just for animals with salvage value.”.

Industry observers note that in the only program one Kenyan participant had worked on with donkeys included, they got rabies vaccination and no food. The rest of the animals were counted for supplementary feeding.

Sources indicate that participants also noted that droughts are far more frequent than before. Money often comes towards the end, when much has died.

Pastoralists summed this up in their own words: “money comes with the vultures.”.

Dr. Emily Haddy, lead author of the paper, did the work at Portsmouth and is now at the University of Nottingham.

“Recognising donkeys in livestock and disaster planning is not just an animal welfare issue,” said Haddy.

“By including working donkeys in drought preparedness and emergency responses, governments and aid organisations can help protect animal welfare and strengthen community resilience.”.

Industry observers note that the veterinarians taking part spoke of getting little or no training on donkeys. One participant in Kenya stated they try to extrapolate from horses, which does not always hold.

“We try to extrapolate what we know from the horse to the donkey, which is not always true,” the participant mentioned.

Sources indicate that vets specializing in donkeys are few and tend to be in urban areas such as Nairobi. Pastoralist communities therefore often have no access, and lose animals that could have been treated.

Medications suitable for donkeys are also in short supply, particularly anesthesia and pain relief.

“I don’t even think there is any firm in Kenya which makes feeds for donkeys,” another participant noted.

Sources indicate that it should be noted the vets interviewed were older graduates. Donkey medicine in the Kenyan vet curriculum has recently improved, though its effect on the ground may take time.

According to participants, the priority for government is animals bringing in foreign currency directly, through sale of meat and hides.

Sources indicate that the services of a donkey are largely invisible. That makes them hard to quantify and keeps them out of national economic reports.

Industry observers note that one participant described a child-focused relief scheme for milk. Donkeys play a vital role in that milk chain, but they were not taken into account.

“They see the human being first, and they see the cattle, the producer of the milk, and the consumer of the milk, the in-between connection they don’t see,” the participant remarked.

Donkey deaths are also not systematically recorded, so they usually do not appear when authorities list the animals that died.

In a recent development, international guidelines do mention working equids. The Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards, aimed at livestock projects in humanitarian crises, include them as pack animals.

The World Organisation for Animal Health gives advice on managing equids during feed shortage too. These were poorly reflected in the national documents.

Professor Tesfaheywet Zeryehun of Haramaya University put the two kinds of welfare side by side.

“Our findings reinforce the fact that donkey welfare cannot be separated from human wellbeing,” stated Zeryehun.

“In drought-prone communities, protecting working donkeys is equally about protecting the livelihoods, resilience and dignity of the families who depend on them.”.

“Their contribution must therefore be recognized in policies and emergency preparedness programs.”.

Documents had to be online and in English to be included. That likely cut the Ethiopian count, as many are in Amharic.

Recent findings suggest that only one pastoralist representative from Ethiopia was interviewed, so those views are probably underrepresented. Fewer than 15% of participants were women.

People were found by snowballing through the authors’ own contacts, and that could bring some selection bias with it.

What’s missing above all is hard evidence on how much donkeys are worth economically. Several interviewees felt numbers on that are what would capture the minds of policy makers.

In a recent development, the authors recommend that equids be explicitly included in livestock definitions. Doing that would make donkeys eligible for the feed and veterinary support that other livestock can get.

They also suggest fodder reserves kept for donkeys, donkey modules in vet training and welfare laws that are actually enforced.

The impact of severe drought on donkey health is named as a research priority.

In a recent development, dr. David Obiero of Maasai Mara University said the gaps reach beyond policy itself.

“The lack of recognition of working donkeys extends beyond policy into veterinary training, access to healthcare and vaccination programmes,” remarked Obiero.

According to recent reports, “These animals are vital to community livelihoods, yet the systems designed to support livestock often overlook them. Addressing these gaps is essential to supporting pastoralist communities during time of drought and beyond.”.

With recurrent droughts expected to intensify, the animal fetching the water is still largely outside the aims to help.

The full study was published in the Journal of Rural Studies.

The libido drug women want is testosterone

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It has been revealed that these days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone.
  • Industry observers note that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that these days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Industry observers note that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih says. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

According to recent reports, the hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen says.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

According to recent reports, women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Rowen presently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for newly introduced treatments is there, Rowen claims. “Women deserve better than placebo.”.

Latest Update: Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress.
  • As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.
  • Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her upcoming colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”.

According to recent reports, not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Sources indicate that rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan noted.

As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

It has been revealed that not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” noted Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number said otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat right now held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”.

Some members revealed their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

“First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” remarked Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”.

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he stated of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The fossil fuel industry is the largest contributor to climate change, and it’s not even close. According to the United Nations, the industry is responsible for 68 percent of all greenhouse gas emissions and an incredible 90 percent of all carbon dioxide emissions. Stick a stake in the vampiric heart of fossil fuels, and beating back the worst effects of global warming becomes suddenly much more possible. But as the recent climate summit at Antalya, Türkiye, this month displayed, the industry demonstrates no interest in giving up its polluting ways, leading some countries to say the world is now “held hostage by the oil mafia.”.

Sources indicate that despite this unwillingness to change, some companies are trying to find ways to make some good out of a bad situation. One of those companies AIRCO (originally named Air Firm), based out of Latest Britain, Pennsylvania, did just that by developing a technology that creates jet fuel of a thin “air”—well, kind of.

Recent findings suggest that instead of making fuel at a massive refinery and transporting it long distances, the system is designed to produce fully formulated synthetic jet or diesel fuel closer to where it will be used,” Nick Steinke, the manufacturer’s director of programs, government and defense, remarked in a recent interview with Waste360. “It takes captured CO₂ and hydrogen and integrates the conversion process into a modular, containerized system.”.

In a recent development, instead of relying on centralized fuel producers, the idea is that synthetic fuels could be created on-site where they’ll be used directly, circumventing the climate impacts of transporting the fuel entirely. Also the ingredients AIRCO uses also aims to come from green sources by leveraging carbon capture technologies for the required CO2 and using electrolysis to supply hydrogen from water.

Industry observers note that chemical & Engineering News reported earlier this year the manufacturer hopes to supply the U.S. military with a complete reactor system by 2027 that will be powered on a government site using a small nuclear reactor (SMR), and supply a sufficient flow of energy required for both carbon capture and electrolysis to provide the volumes of ingredients needed to make these mobile, fuel-creating systems viable. It’s a task that at least one expert indicates sounds easier noted than done.

“The technology seems like it holds a lot of promise, especially on the fuel-conversion side, but the part that I have a lot of questions about is, where are you getting the carbon from?” Sarah Gleeson, a materials scientist at Project Drawdown, told WHYY, a local radio station. “Because if they’re saying that there’s some kind of direct air capture functionality in this really mobile device, I would be skeptical at the capacity and efficiency of it.”.

Carbon capture is central to the tech giant’s promise of its technology’s carbon-neutral nature with the company’s CEO telling WHYY that “using more CO2 in our production process to make the fuel than we are putting out in the entire process.” Carbon capture, as a broad technology category, still remains unproved even as some climate models rely on its implementation (and the fact that the oil industry likes the technology is concerning to say the least).

Recent findings suggest that if humanity hopes to secure a healthy planet for future generations, ending its reliance on fossil fuels is priority number one. But step one in the process is first limiting—and eventually eliminating— fresh fuel from being extracted from the ground in the first place while the advancements in green chemistry try to put to work the carbon dioxide that’s already here.

#135516. Industry News: Artificial intelligence could fundamentally change how we grow our food

Industry News: Artificial intelligence could fundamentally change how we grow our food

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new review explores how generative AI could transform crop breeding and help address future agricultural challenges.
  • Recent findings suggest that modern plant breeding runs on genome data and decades of catalogued crop genes.
  • Conventional crossbreeding largely relies on existing genetic variation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new review explores how generative AI could transform crop breeding and help address future agricultural challenges.

Recent findings suggest that modern plant breeding runs on genome data and decades of catalogued crop genes. For all that, it still takes 10 to 15 years to turn a promising cross into a variety a farmer can plant.

Conventional crossbreeding largely relies on existing genetic variation.

A newly introduced review states the next round of breeding won’t start with a plant at all. It will start with a model that writes DNA no plant has ever carried, and a lab that builds the sequence to see whether it works.

Feng Xu, Jun Yan, Xiangfeng Wang and their colleagues at China Agricultural University went through 67 generative AI tools built for biological design.

They sorted the tools by the part of breeding each one could serve, and hardly any were made with crops in mind.

Most were trained on microbes or mammalian cells, and the authors wrote that carrying them over to a maize or wheat genome is unfinished work.

The appeal lies in what the older tools couldn’t do.

Yield that holds up in a dry year is controlled by many genes at once, and a model that only ranks the variants nature supplied has a short reach.

Plant breeders mark their own history in stages, and the review counts four before this one. Choosing by eye and crossing came first.

Molecular markers came next, then genomic selection, then the omics work of the past decade, which filled catalogs with crop genes and the traits attached to them.

Every stage improved the odds of picking well. None of them changed the basic move, which was to choose among variation that already existed in a species.

Breeders have worked those catalogs for particular traits, from tomato flavor to seed size to crops that fertilize themselves.

Breeding 5.0, the authors’ name for what comes next, is meant to change the move itself. Design the genetic part first, then build it.

In a recent development, artificial intelligence in plant science has mostly sorted things. It scored variants, predicted traits and ranked candidates a breeder could already have grown.

Industry observers note that generative models work the other way around. Trained on enough DNA and protein structures, they produce newly introduced examples that fit the patterns they learned.

That buys two things the authors care about: sequences beyond anything in nature, and screening that happens before a seed goes in the ground.

It has been revealed that four kinds of model do most of this work. One compresses sequences into a map a researcher can move through in small steps, which suits fine-tuning how strongly a gene switches on.

One trains two networks against each other. The first writes sequences, and the second tries to spot the fakes.

A third starts from noise and strips it away a step at a time, which gives tight control over three-dimensional shapes.

The fourth treats DNA as a language, with bases as letters and genes as sentences.

Those language models are the ones that can take an instruction in plain words.

The clearest results involve the short stretches of DNA that decide when a gene switches on and how strongly. Biologists call them promoters.

In cyanobacteria, 95% of the promoters one model designed turned out to be active. In E. coli, a second model wrote promoters that worked 70.8% of the time and looked little like anything in nature.

The authors call that design from scratch. Designs can be tuned as well as built. A third model raised promoter activity by as much as 33.43-fold, and in yeast a fourth moved expression across a thousandfold range.

In a recent development, of that fourth model’s designs, 57% beat the strongest natural promoters they were measured against. Not one of those organisms is a crop.

It has been revealed that that pattern runs through the review. The proof exists, and it exists in microbes. Plant-specific models are appearing, and most of them still score sequences instead of writing them.

Genome editing lets breeders change a gene directly, and Cas9, the enzyme behind most of that work, came out of bacteria.

Profluent Bio fine-tuned a protein language model until it produced OpenCRISPR-1, the first openly available Cas9 designed this way.

It cut DNA about as well as the standard enzyme, with better specificity, and it still read the short tag that marks where to cut. A separate model produced another Cas9 variant that worked in mammalian cells.

Protein design has gone further outside plants. One model produced 310 proteins that folded as predicted once made, and tools like AlphaFold made that check routine.

In plants, almost all the published work is redesign of existing proteins, including a refined enzyme in Arabidopsis and an improved potato protein.

The authors stated design from scratch has rarely been validated in crops.

The authors also raised safety and regulatory questions about AI-designed proteins in crops, including their potential unintended effects, how long they persist under field conditions, and whether they are safe to consume.

So the authors suggested starting small, with designed proteins used as laboratory probes rather than put straight into a crop.

The authors’ own contribution is a framework they call DESIGN, named for six capabilities: discover, engineer, simulate, integrate, generate and navigate.

In plainer words, find the patterns in existing data and pull together information of different kinds.

Then design molecules that fit a set of constraints, make parts nature does not, test candidates in simulation, and weigh competing goals.

Industry observers note that the authors set out two worked cases. One designs a maize promoter that stays quiet in a watered field and drives a drought-response gene hard when water runs short.

The other designs a protein that traps a molecule the stripe rust fungus uses to switch off the defenses of wheat.

It has been revealed that neither case is a finished experiment. Both are plans, detailed enough to name the tool at each step and the filter a candidate must clear.

The six capabilities don’t run in a line, the authors wrote. They run as a loop: learn, design, build, test, then feed the results back into the model.

It has been revealed that three problems sit between the framework and a field. Plant datasets are scattered across species and growing conditions, and well-annotated ones are thin for most crops.

Recent findings suggest that many models don’t transfer between domains or explain their output. Testing in plants is slow, so designs pile up faster than anyone can check them.

Plant genomes make the data problem worse, being larger and more repetitive than the genomes most of these models learned from.

It has been revealed that the same gap highlights up in single-cell work. One plant model, built for Arabidopsis, labeled cell types it had never been shown with 0.91 accuracy.

The goal is to simulate how a root cell handles salty soil before planting.

Sources indicate that the authors emphasized that AI is not meant to replace plant breeders. Breeders will continue to set agricultural goals and evaluate real-world results, while AI helps explore new possibilities.

What hasn’t happened yet, by the authors’ own accounting, is the validation of even one designed protein or regulatory element in a greenhouse or a field.

They named the benchmarks and shared datasets that would get the field there. That greenhouse result is the thing to watch for.

The full study was published in the journal Science China Life Sciences.

#135514. An overlooked brain region offers fresh clues to how memory works

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1003 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

An overlooked brain region offers fresh clues to how memory works

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In mice, a thin brain sheet called the claustrum kept a smell or a touch in working memory for 30 seconds, and quieting it cut performance.
  • Anyone following a conversation holds the last sentence in mind while the next one arrives.
  • Part of that job, at least in mice, belongs to a sliver of nerve cells wedged between the cortex and the structures beneath it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In mice, a thin brain sheet called the claustrum kept a smell or a touch in working memory for 30 seconds, and quieting it cut performance.

Anyone following a conversation holds the last sentence in mind while the next one arrives. The sound is gone within a moment, yet the brain keeps using it for seconds, and where it keeps it is only partly understood.

Part of that job, at least in mice, belongs to a sliver of nerve cells wedged between the cortex and the structures beneath it.

It has been revealed that the sliver is called the claustrum. In mice, it kept a trace of a smell or a touch for up to 30 seconds. Quieting it cut the animals’ scores on a memory task by roughly 40% to 60%.

Alan Carleton and Ivan Rodriguez of the University of Geneva led the work, with Anindya Bhattacharjee as first author.

Carleton’s lab in the Department of Basic Neurosciences studies how the brain handles the senses, and the claustrum caught the team’s attention because of its wiring.

“Its neurons are connected to almost all regions of the cortex, which puts it in a good position to receive and influence information from very different networks,” Carleton remarked.

The short-term hold the study tested is called working memory. Reading and deciding both depend on it, and it is impaired in disorders such as schizophrenia and ADHD.

It runs on brain circuits spread across many regions, and how those circuits hold information over time isn’t clear.

The team trained head-fixed mice on a game of same or different.

A tone marked the start of each trial. Then came a one-second cue. It was one of two odors, or a puff of air on the left or right whiskers.

Sources indicate that after a delay of 5 to 60 seconds, a second cue arrived. If it differed from the first, the mouse earned a drop of water by licking a tube. If it matched, licking earned nothing.

Recent findings suggest that thirty mice learned the odor version, and within about 400 trials they were scoring above 70%. Twenty-three of the 25 mice given the whisker version learned it too.

Sources indicate that scores fell as the delay grew. The memory faded at the same rate for both senses, with a half-life of about 20 seconds in the typical mouse.

In a recent development, in seven mice, the team watched claustrum cells through a tiny lens while the animals played. Each cell carried a sensor that glows when the cell is active.

About a quarter of the cells fired at the cue, and about 60% fired during the wait. Roughly a quarter responded to one cue but not the other.

The cells’ activity shifted as the wait went on. Even so, a computer program reading the whole population could still tell which cue the mouse had received, right up to the second cue, at every delay tested.

On trials the mouse got wrong, the program did far worse.

Recent findings suggest that “Far from being a static memory, neuronal activity changed over time,” Rodriguez said. “Nevertheless, the identity of the stimulus remained sufficiently present to be decoded up to 30 seconds later.”.

Only a small share of the cells tracked licking or movements of the nose, mouth or forepaw, about 8% at most for any one of them.

The findings suggest that the memory trace was not simply a reflection of the animal’s movements.

To test whether the claustrum was needed, the team dialed its cells down in two ways. A drug that acts only on cells carrying an engineered receptor cut scores by about 40%.

Optogenetics, in which cells carry a light-sensitive protein and a fiber delivers light for about one second, cut them by 40% to 60%.

The light trials were mixed in with ordinary trials in the same session, and performance suffered regardless of when the light was delivered.

Dimming the claustrum during the first cue, early in the wait, late in the wait or during the second cue hurt in every case.

“The result was similar regardless of the type of stimulus, olfactory or tactile, and regardless of when the disruption occurred during the waiting period between the two stimuli,” Carleton stated.

Mice carrying a harmless protein instead of the light-sensitive one played as well with the light on as off.

The same mice then played a version with no delay, telling two odors or two puffs apart on the spot. The light had no effect on that.

According to recent reports, the mice’s pupils, body movements and licking looked the same with and without it, and they didn’t lick early during long waits. What fell was the rate of correct licks on trials where the cues differed.

“Disrupting the claustrum specifically impairs the ability to use temporarily held information to guide behavior, without affecting perception itself,” Carleton said.

The sliver is thin and poorly bounded, so the team could only partly quiet it, and the mice still scored well above chance. Other regions carry short-term memories too, and this study doesn’t say how the work is shared.

It has been revealed that A second team reported in June on a set of cells in and around the claustrum that connect to the prefrontal cortex. Mice needed those cells while holding a location in mind in a maze.

Silencing them during the decision itself improved performance, the opposite of what the Geneva team saw.

The two groups used different tasks and targeted different cells, and neither result settles which cells do what.

How the claustrum keeps a memory steady while its own activity drifts is the open question.

The next step, Carleton mentioned, is to work out how the claustrum talks to the cortex, and how that exchange keeps a held memory from degrading.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.
