Violent star collisions may have created the earliest giant black holes

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1466 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crowded early star clusters could merge stars into one giant, and a latest model shows how that giant may become a black hole seed.
  • According to recent reports, space is so empty that two stars almost never hit each other.
  • A new model suggests those crashes could merge stars until one carried the mass of the whole cluster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crowded early star clusters could merge stars into one giant, and a latest model shows how that giant may become a black hole seed.

According to recent reports, space is so empty that two stars almost never hit each other. In the first star clusters, though, stars were packed so tightly that they may have crashed into one another again and again.

A new model suggests those crashes could merge stars until one carried the mass of the whole cluster. A star that heavy may have no way to die except by collapsing into a black hole.

That matters because the James Webb Space Telescope keeps finding enormous black holes far earlier in cosmic history than astronomers expected.

It has been revealed that the newly introduced work, led by Claire Williams, a doctoral student at UCLA, is a calculation rather than an observation. It maps where colliding stars could have made the seeds of those black holes.

Webb’s deep images show extremely compact star clusters in the early universe, and computer simulations of that era produce the same crowding.

Williams and her colleagues in the UCLA Division of Astronomy and Astrophysics built a model to ask what happens to the stars inside them.

Co-authors of the study came from Northwestern’s CIERA and seven other institutions.

The model clusters ranged from about two-thirds of a light-year in radius to roughly 300 light-years.

In a recent development, they held anywhere from ten thousand to a billion times the mass of the Sun. Some had a black hole at the center and some did not.

It has been revealed that for each one, the team worked out how often stars would run into each other before something stopped them. That could be the stars burning out or a neighboring clump of matter crashing in.

It has been revealed that even with the strictest assumptions, collisions should have been common in many of these systems. Test simulations tracking 1,000 individual stars near a cluster’s center agreed on where they happen.

In a recent development, in an interview with Earth.com, Williams mentioned star collisions matter today only in rare, extreme places, such as the cores of galaxies. So astronomers usually don’t treat them as central to how stars live.

“We were surprised to discover how ubiquitous these collisions might have been,” she mentioned.

Sources indicate that what a collision does depends on how fast the two stars meet. If they meet at speeds below the escape speed at a star’s surface, they can merge into one bigger star.

At higher speeds, collisions can strip material from both stars or destroy them entirely, releasing gas from their interiors.

In a cluster with no black hole, the model found no system where stars moved fast enough to destroy each other. Every collision was a merger.

And because the merged stars are heavier than their neighbors, they sink toward the center swiftly, where they collide again.

“Perhaps the strangest outcome of our simulations is that stars can merge repeatedly within the cluster until they form one gigantic star with a mass equal to that of an entire cluster,” Williams said.

“When a star this huge reaches the end of its life, models suggest that it may have no option but to collapse into itself and form a massive black hole.”.

How big that merged star gets depends mostly on how tightly the cluster is packed.

In the model’s standard setup, the central star passes 200 times the Sun’s mass only once a cluster holds roughly 100,000 suns’ worth of stars per cubic parsec. A parsec is about 3.3 light-years.

Industry observers note that above that line, nearly all of the lightest clusters in the model produced one. In the densest cases, the merged star passed 100,000 solar masses.

In a recent development, when the team filled the clusters with heavy stars instead of Sun-like ones, only 22 systems built a giant at all, and the largest reached 512 solar masses. Heavy stars burn out promptly, so the collisions ran out of time.

If each giant collapses into a black hole of the same mass, the result is an intermediate-mass black hole, a size astronomers have struggled to find.

Other groups have already proposed stellar mergers as a route to early black holes, and the team’s giant-star masses broadly agree with theirs.

The fresh part is one framework that runs from an ordinary early cluster to a black hole star wrapped in gas.

Sources indicate that once a black hole is at the center, the outcome changes. Its gravity speeds up the stars closest to it, so collisions there happen too fast to merge.

The stars are torn apart instead, and the gas from their interiors piles up in a tiny region around the black hole.

The Milky Way’s center is the nearby example. “One place in the nearby universe where collisions between stars are common is the galactic center,” Williams remarked.

“In our model, once these very massive stars turn into intermediate-mass black holes, the system resembles our own galactic center, which is a black hole surrounded by a dense star cluster.”.

That dense, gassy core is why the authors connect the model to Webb’s little red dots.

Astronomers believe these compact objects hold a rapidly growing black hole, and several recent studies describe that black hole as buried in dense gas.

In the model, a cluster as dense as a little red dot would build a central star of 10,000 to 100,000 solar masses. Once a black hole formed, collisions would keep feeding gas toward it.

Williams mentioned other researchers had already proposed that very massive stars might be connected to the dots.

“Little Red Dots may represent the densest extreme of a continuum of stellar systems that formed naturally in the early Universe, rather than an entirely separate class of object,” she told Earth.com.

Smadar Naoz, a UCLA astrophysicist and co-author, compared the research on the dots to the tale of blind people each describing an elephant by the part they touch.

“Our research connects several of those perspectives together and may help us see more of the elephant,” Naoz said.

Asked by Earth.com what Webb could see to confirm the picture, Williams stated there may not be a single “smoking gun.”.

The most direct test, she remarked, is spectroscopy, which splits an object’s light into its component wavelengths.

The bright and dark lines in that spectrum reveal the temperature, chemical makeup and motion of the material giving off the light.

With better theoretical predictions, those lines could help tell light from very massive stars apart from light reworked by gas around a black hole that is actively feeding.

Industry observers note that one clue would be unusual amounts of certain elements, thrown out when collisions expose the insides of stars. The gas from these collisions may be unusually rich in nitrogen, which has already turned up in some early clusters.

A second test would look for leftovers. If collisions built very massive stars that later collapsed, some of the resulting black holes may now wander near the edges of galaxies.

In a newer preprint that has not been peer reviewed, Williams’s team reports that upcoming sky surveys could find them.

Surveys by the Rubin Observatory and the Roman Space Telescope may spot the black holes when they destroy stars that pass too close.

“Finding a larger population of these events would provide independent evidence that dense early clusters formed intermediate-mass black holes through runaway stellar collisions,” Williams noted.

The authors list what their simplified model leaves out. It ignores any gas left over from the cluster’s birth, which they expect would pull merged stars inward even faster.

It doesn’t update the stars’ masses as mergers happen, so it may miss runaway growth.

Its estimate of how much material a fast collision strips from a star is also likely too high. So the gas densities around black holes may be overstated.

The model also stops at the giant star. It doesn’t follow whether that star collapses, how much of its mass ends up inside a black hole, or how fast the black hole grows afterward.

In a recent development, williams said the team’s next step is following the gas that fast collisions throw into the middle of a cluster. The current model estimates how much gas that makes, but not where it goes.

It has been revealed that the gas could stay trapped, cool and feed the black hole, change the orbits of nearby stars, or be driven out. Each outcome would leave a different signature for telescopes to look for.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal.

Latest Update: Exploding stars were supposed to free light from early galaxies, but they may have done the opposite

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hubble spectra of six young galaxies suggest winds from exploding stars trapped the light that drove the reionization of the Universe, rather than freeing it.
  • For most of its first billion years, the Universe was wrapped in a fog of hydrogen gas that blocked ultraviolet light.
  • Astronomers have long assumed that exploding stars helped, by blasting open channels for light to get out of young galaxies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hubble spectra of six young galaxies suggest winds from exploding stars trapped the light that drove the reionization of the Universe, rather than freeing it.

For most of its first billion years, the Universe was wrapped in a fog of hydrogen gas that blocked ultraviolet light. Something cleared that fog.

Astronomers have long assumed that exploding stars helped, by blasting open channels for light to get out of young galaxies.

Newly introduced Hubble observations of six nearby galaxies point the other way: the galaxies leaking the most light were the ones whose stars hadn’t started exploding yet.

Cody Carr led the study as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China and is now a postdoctoral researcher in astronomy at the University of Michigan.

Renyue Cen of Zhejiang and Stephan McCandliss of Johns Hopkins University were the senior authors, and nearly 30 researchers from more than a dozen institutions took part.

“Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn’t what we thought,” Carr mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that in the early Universe, hydrogen atoms were whole, each a proton with an electron attached. Gas like that soaks up ultraviolet light.

It has been revealed that high-energy light from the first galaxies eventually knocked the electrons off, and gas in that state is transparent. Astronomers call the change reionization, and Carr described it as the last major phase transition of the Universe.

The puzzle has been how the light got out, because a galaxy forming stars at a furious rate is also full of gas and dust that absorb that light.

In a recent development, one long-standing answer involved supernovae, the explosions that end the lives of the biggest stars. Their winds, the idea went, pushed the gas aside and opened the way.

It has been revealed that the alternative is that the light escaped earlier, while the biggest stars were still alive. Their own radiation and the fast winds blowing off their surfaces would have done the work, before any star had exploded.

Galaxies from the early Universe are too faint and too far away to study in this detail, so the team picked six nearby galaxies that resemble them.

Recent findings suggest that all six are compact and forming stars at a high rate, and all six have similar mass and chemical makeup. What differs is how much of their high-energy light escapes – from less than 0.4 percent to about 21 percent.

The team used the Hubble Space Telescope to take deep spectra of each one, spreading the ultraviolet light into its component wavelengths.

Gas moving toward us absorbs light at slightly shifted wavelengths, so the dips in a spectrum show how fast a galaxy’s wind is blowing and how much gas it carries.

The spectra also show how old each galaxy’s current burst of star formation is. The biggest stars live only a few million years before they explode, so a burst younger than about three million years has no supernovae yet.

The three galaxies leaking the most light were the youngest, with bursts under about four million years old.

In the youngest of all, the absorption came mostly from the fast winds blowing off massive stars, at around 6.7 million miles per hour (3,000 kilometers per second). The galaxy-wide wind was slow.

The three weakest leakers were older, and their spectra looked different. The stellar-wind signature had faded, and a galaxy-wide wind had taken over, carrying more neutral hydrogen and more dust.

In the youngest galaxy that wind moved at roughly 335,000 miles per hour (150 kilometers per second). The oldest galaxies drove winds about five times faster.

The faster the wind, the less light got out. The authors read that as the launch of a wind, driven by exploding stars, that sweeps gas and dust up into the outflow, where it blocks the light that had been escaping.

“It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape,” McCandliss mentioned.

According to recent reports, the team checked whether the pattern holds beyond six galaxies. They stacked the spectra of 89 galaxies from a larger Hubble survey into three groups by how much light escapes.

The strongest leakers demonstrated narrower hydrogen absorption than the rest, in line with slower winds, and the non-leakers hosted the fastest winds.

The timing changes the arithmetic of reionization. A galaxy’s contribution depends on how much high-energy light it makes and what fraction gets out, and those two things can peak at different times.

If the light escapes while the biggest stars are still alive and shining, galaxies like these could have done more of the work than models that wait for supernovae allow.

Industry observers note that simulations that explain reionization lean heavily on supernovae. Cen noted the results point to a need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode.

Industry observers note that six galaxies is a small sample. The ages come from fitting models to the starlight, so the timeline is an average rather than a clock. Hubble’s spectra also can’t see the hottest wind gas, which only shows up in X-rays.

The team looked for X-rays from the strongest leaker with a separate telescope and found none. That fits a galaxy whose supernova-driven wind hasn’t started.

The six galaxies are also heavier and richer in heavy elements than the galaxies of the first billion years.

In a recent development, in lighter, more primitive galaxies, the authors expect radiation to matter even more. Massive stars there are likelier to collapse into black holes without exploding, which would delay the supernova winds further.

Whether compact galaxies like these were enough to clear the fog on their own is still an open question. Carr and his colleagues are seeking more Hubble time to observe more galaxies.

The 36-year-old telescope is near the end of its working life, the authors wrote. The proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory is one instrument that could take over this kind of measurement.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

#135508. Electrons usually flow freely through metals, but Columbia scientists just found a way to trap them in place

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Electrons usually flow freely through metals, but Columbia scientists just found a way to trap them in place

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicists trapped electrons at a missing atom inside a metal crystal, where quantum interference left them no route out.
  • Sources indicate that A metal conducts electricity because its electrons spread through the whole crystal, the way a ripple spreads across a pond rather than staying where it started.
  • However, in a palladium compound made at Columbia University, two of them hold still anyway, pinned to a single missing atom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicists trapped electrons at a missing atom inside a metal crystal, where quantum interference left them no route out.

Sources indicate that A metal conducts electricity because its electrons spread through the whole crystal, the way a ripple spreads across a pond rather than staying where it started. There’s nowhere in a metal for one to hold still.

However, in a palladium compound made at Columbia University, two of them hold still anyway, pinned to a single missing atom.

Morgan Thinel, Simon Turkel and colleagues in Columbia’s Department of Physics and Department of Chemistry found them with a microscope that feels a surface atom by atom.

Two of the authors also work at Brookhaven National Laboratory, and the group’s theorists reproduced both states on paper.

Recent findings suggest that the trap is not a wall around the electron. It is the metal crystal’s own geometry cancelling every route out.

In a recent development, the material is Pd5AlI2, a palladium-aluminum-iodine compound that Xavier Roy’s chemistry group at Columbia built a few years ago. It is a van der Waals crystal, which means it comes apart into sheets the way graphite does, and the sheets stay metallic.

The compound’s electrons moved more slowly than anyone expected, and the group published the reason last year. Call it gridlock: an electron has competing routes to the next atom, and the routes cancel.

The cancelling is the whole mechanism here. A quantum particle does not take one path; it takes every available path at once.

It has been revealed that the paths add up like waves, reinforcing in some directions and wiping each other out in others. When the wiping-out is complete, there is no route out at all.

Industry observers note that physicists call the result a bound state in the continuum. The particle is stuck in place even though it is surrounded by an unbroken range of energies into which it could escape.

Light does this. Over the past decade, engineers have etched patterns into materials to catch photons that way, and the trick now drives lasers and sensors. In a metal, it had stayed out of reach.

The team split a crystal open in vacuum and cooled it to about 7 degrees above absolute zero. Then a scanning tunneling microscope measured how easily electrons flow into the surface, point by point and energy by energy.

It has been revealed that across a clean stretch, the answer was much the same everywhere, which is what a metal crystal looks like. Over one kind of flaw in the lattice, two sharp peaks appeared. One sat 475 millivolts above the metal’s own energy floor and the other 620.

It has been revealed that comparing the images with simulations identified the flaw: a single palladium atom missing from the layer buried inside each sheet. Vacancies like it turned up across the crystal at roughly two trillion per square centimeter.

In a recent development, both states hug the vacancy inside a single nanometer, a span a few atoms wide. A normal defect in a metal only nudges the passing electron waves. These two were not passing.

“Bound electrons shouldn’t occur in a metal, but they do in Pd5AlI2,” stated Raquel Queiroz, a theoretical physicist at Columbia who built the models behind the result.

“What we have observed is the first clear evidence of quantum interference trapping a state in a metal.”.

It has been revealed that mapping each peak across the surface produced two pictures. The lower one has four lobes, like a clover. The upper one is a plain circle.

Those are the shapes of orbitals around a single atom, which is an odd thing to find around an absence.

Recent findings suggest that the team’s model is a stripped-down version of the layer with one atom removed. It produced both shapes, and put them a few hundred millivolts above the energy floor, where the microscope found them.

The circular one only appears once the model includes the iodine atoms sitting above and below the gap.

The team also answered the obvious objection. The gridlock in an idealized version of this lattice is perfect, and perfect conditions are not what a real crystal offers.

Loosening the model so the electrons are not quite frozen keeps the two states tightly bound across a wide range of settings, including the ones that match the real material.

In a recent development, when two palladium atoms were missing from neighboring sites, the pair of states became four. Each of the original two had split, into a slightly lower energy and a slightly higher one.

Recent findings suggest that that is what happens when two atoms bond into a molecule. The resemblance runs even further. For the four-lobed state, the lower version piles electron density between the two gaps at 440 millivolts. The higher one, at 510, leaves the middle empty.

Move the vacancies two lattice spacings apart and the splitting disappears.

So the trapped states behave like the orbitals of atoms that are not there, and two of them nearby make something like a molecule out of two holes.

It has been revealed that no one is placing these on purpose yet. Every vacancy here arrived by chance while the crystal was growing.

That is the sharpest difference from the light version of the effect, where the pattern goes exactly where the designer wants it. Roy’s and Abhay Pasupathy’s groups are working on putting flaws where they choose.

What a trapped electron is good for is also open. The authors note that photonic bound states have essentially unlimited lifetimes, and suggest these might carry charge without loss at their own energies, but nothing here measured current through one.

Sources indicate that “And if you trap a particle, you can manipulate it,” Roy said. The uses he and his colleagues point to, from quantum sensors to quantum computers, are a long way past what was measured.

It has been revealed that the prediction worth testing is that the lattice did this, not the material. If gridlocked hopping is the ingredient, other crystals with the same frustrated geometry should trap electrons the same way.

According to recent reports, the authors name two common lattice patterns to look at next. That is a recipe, and the next paper either finds one or does not.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

Rep. James Comer rolls out 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

💡 Key Takeaways
  • James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor.
  • Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has introduced a run for governor next year.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has introduced a run for governor next year.

Recent findings suggest that the Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook concerns, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

In a recent development, as the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.).

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

It has been revealed that known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Comer has moved swiftly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

Sources indicate that while Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”.

Sources indicate that while Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”.

It was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

Sources indicate that in September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

Sources indicate that all that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

It has been revealed that 2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the New Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

Sources indicate that the heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

#135505. Industry News: Dams may be getting blamed for carbon emissions that would occur naturally

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1079 w)

Industry News: Dams may be getting blamed for carbon emissions that would occur naturally

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A global study suggests that conventional carbon accounting may substantially overestimate certain greenhouse gas emissions directly attributable to dams.
  • When a river is dammed, decomposing organic matter in the resulting reservoir can release carbon dioxide and methane.
  • Sources indicate that that is why reservoirs now sit in national greenhouse gas inventories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A global study suggests that conventional carbon accounting may substantially overestimate certain greenhouse gas emissions directly attributable to dams.

When a river is dammed, decomposing organic matter in the resulting reservoir can release carbon dioxide and methane.

Sources indicate that that is why reservoirs now sit in national greenhouse gas inventories. It is also why some people question hydropower’s green credentials.

But much of the organic carbon carried into reservoirs would have decomposed naturally in rivers and estuaries even without dams.

A fresh study estimates that dams add about 21.5% to the emissions from the carbon they trap, once a free-flowing river’s own emissions are counted.

For the type of carbon tracked in the study, the net emissions attributable to dams were less than a fifth of conventional estimates.

The research was led by Wenqing Shi of Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology.

The co-authors came from the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, the University of North Carolina’s Institute of Marine Sciences, and Aarhus University in Denmark.

“High carbon emissions from reservoirs have sparked controversy over dams,” the team wrote.

In an interview with Earth.com, Shi noted that a fair test compares the same river with and without the dam, from the reservoir down to the estuary.

“We need to distinguish emissions that occur in a reservoir from emissions actually added by the dam,” Shi said.

Rivers carry about 940 million tons (850 million metric tons) of land-grown carbon to the ocean every year. Some of it decays in the channel on the way down.

Most of it settles in estuaries, where it decays too, releasing the same two gases.

In a recent development, A dam interrupts the trip. More than 70,000 large dams now stand on the world’s rivers, and each one catches carbon that would otherwise have kept moving.

Sources indicate that the usual accounting charges every ton of gas rising from a reservoir to the dam that made it. That treats the carbon as if it would have stayed put without the dam.

Shi’s team ran the numbers both ways for 5,346 dammed reservoirs around the world: once with the dam in place, and once with the river flowing freely to the sea.

It has been revealed that methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide, so the team converted it to a carbon dioxide equivalent, at 27.2 times the warming over a century. That put the two scenarios on one scale.

The two rivers look very different. In the free-flowing version, about 4.9% of the carbon decays in the channel and the rest reaches the estuary.

In the dammed version, 88.3% of the carbon arriving from upstream is caught in the reservoir, 0.5% decays in the channel below, and 11.1% makes it to the estuary.

Recent findings suggest that nearly every dam, 99.4% of them, raised emissions compared with the undammed river. The average increase was 21.5%, and the team’s uncertainty range runs from 8.3% to 32.6%.

The conventional method counts all reservoir emissions as the dam’s doing. Measured against it, the net effect is 18.6% of the old figure.

“We expected the baseline to matter, but the size of the difference was striking,” Shi told Earth.com.

Shi emphasized that the 18.6% figure covers only the land-grown carbon particles the study followed, not every source of reservoir emissions or hydropower’s whole carbon footprint.

“The emissions themselves have not disappeared; what changes is how much can reasonably be attributed to the dam,” Shi said.

Added up, the world’s dams release an extra 6 million tons (5.4 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide equivalent a year, by the team’s estimate.

Hydroelectric dams account for just over half of that, with irrigation dams next and flood control dams third.

Per ton of trapped carbon, hydroelectric dams add the least, 16.5% against more than 19.4% for every other dam type. They lead the list because there are so many of them and they drain such large areas.

A few dams even cut emissions. On rivers flowing from cool regions toward warm coasts, carbon held back in cold water decays more slowly than it would in a warm estuary.

Sources indicate that what a dam changes most is which gas comes out. In reservoirs, slow water lets organic-rich mud pile up and run out of oxygen, and that is where methane forms.

Free-flowing rivers generally have more oxygenated conditions that are less favorable to methane production.

In the team’s model, methane’s share of the warming from decaying river carbon rose from 4.4% without dams to 22.8% with them, more than a fivefold jump.

“Reservoir conditions can favor methane production, so shifting decomposition upstream can still increase the climate impact, even after accounting for the no-dam baseline,” Shi said.

Reservoir depth and how long water lingers behind the dam were the strongest controls.

Shallow reservoirs and very deep ones both pushed emissions up, while reservoirs between about 65 and 260 feet (20 and 80 meters) deep held them down.

Shi said that spread is one more reason not to apply a single correction factor to every reservoir.

Recent findings suggest that the model follows only one kind of carbon, the particles washed in from the land. It leaves out carbon in soil flooded when a reservoir fills, carbon dissolved in the water, and algae grown in the reservoir itself.

Recent findings suggest that all three can add to a reservoir’s emissions. So the team called its 18.6% a conservative figure, and the true share pinned on dams could be higher.

Those other sources, and hydropower’s full life-cycle impacts, still have to be assessed separately, Shi said.

The researchers also treated all incoming carbon alike, though carbon from different watersheds decays at different rates.

No global dataset yet describes how a dam changes the flow of the river below it, so that effect is missing too.

“A priority is to make the estuary baseline more site-specific,” Shi said. That means measuring the carbon arriving, how much of it is buried or decays, and the gases that come off.

The team also wrote that any carbon accounting for a dam should run from the reservoir all the way to the estuary.

Until that happens, the figure in a hydropower plant’s carbon ledger depends on where the ledger decides the river begins.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#135503. Ice baths don’t help your muscles recover after a workout any better than heat-based methods, according to a new study

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1042 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Ice baths don’t help your muscles recover after a workout any better than heat-based methods, according to a new study

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite the popularity of ice baths for post-workout recovery, latest research finds that cold-water immersion helps restore muscle strength no better than heat-based methods.
  • It has been revealed that enduring a freezing ice bath after a hard workout feels like a steep price to pay for better muscle recovery.
  • In a recent development, for this research project, forty people wrecked one thigh muscle on purpose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite the popularity of ice baths for post-workout recovery, latest research finds that cold-water immersion helps restore muscle strength no better than heat-based methods.

It has been revealed that enduring a freezing ice bath after a hard workout feels like a steep price to pay for better muscle recovery. Now, results from a new study show that cold-water immersion restored strength no faster than sitting in a chair with a hot towel around your neck.

In a recent development, for this research project, forty people wrecked one thigh muscle on purpose. They then spent 15 to 30 minutes in cold water, hot water, hot air, or an ordinary room. Three days later, their strength had come back at the same pace in every group.

The hot water did change the body in ways the ice bath didn’t. Blood markers of muscle damage settled faster after a hot bath, and a protective protein rose more.

Those changes never indicated up as extra strength or less soreness. So, for now, the finding is that heat and cold are different, not that either one is better.

According to recent reports, freya Bayne, a lecturer in sport and exercise science at the University of East London, led the study. Her co-authors came from London South Bank University, Maastricht University, and the University of Montpellier, among others.

Each person got one session of one treatment, and the follow-up stopped at 72 hours, so the results say nothing about weeks of regular ice baths.

“Cold-water immersion remains one of the most popular recovery strategies used by athletes and recreational exercisers alike,” Bayne said.

“Our findings suggest that heat-based recovery methods produce different physiological responses following strenuous exercise, particularly in relation to markers associated with cellular protection and muscle repair.”.

The volunteers were 40 adults, 31 of them men, averaging 26 years old, who already lifted weights three to five hours a week.

Each one sat at a machine that forced the dominant knee to bend while the thigh muscle fought it, 210 times in all. Contractions like that are what make muscles sore a day or two later.

It has been revealed that right after the session, the thigh could push with about 36 percent less force than before. That loss is what the recovery treatments were meant to undo.

Each person was assigned at random to one of four treatments, ten to a group. One group sat chest-deep in water at 108°F (42°C) for 30 minutes, and another sat in an ice bath at 48°F (9°C) for 15 minutes.

A third sat in a room heated to 86°F (30°C) for 30 minutes, and the last sat in a room at 64°F (18°C) in their gym clothes.

In a recent development, everyone came back at 24, 48, and 72 hours to push against the machine again. They also gave blood and rated their pain and soreness.

In a recent development, by 72 hours, the hot water, hot air, and plain room groups had all recovered about 88 to 90 percent of their starting strength. The cold water group was at about 82 percent.

Recent findings suggest that the gap between cold water and the rest looks like something, but with ten people per group the uncertainty around it is wide. The statistics could not separate any group from any other.

The authors wrote that the pattern fits other recent work suggesting cold can slow the signals that rebuild muscle, while stopping short of calling it a result.

Three things in the blood told a different story from the strength test. One was a protein called creatine kinase, which leaks out of damaged muscle fibers.

Sources indicate that it was back to normal 48 hours after the hot bath and 72 hours after hot air or a plain room. After the cold bath, it was still about 25 percent above normal at 72 hours.

Recent findings suggest that the second was heat shock protein 72, a protein that cells make under stress to protect and repair themselves. Right after the treatment, the hot water group’s level was more than three times its start. The cold water group’s was about one and a half times.

The third, an immune messenger called interleukin-6, spiked highest after the hot bath and then dropped fastest, back to near normal within a day.

In a recent development, only the hot bath warmed the muscle itself, from 98°F to 102°F (36.6°C to 38.8°C). The cold bath cooled it to 93°F (34°C).

Pain and soreness rose in every group by the next day and were still up at 72 hours. No treatment brought them back to the starting point. The hot air group reported the most pain on days one and two and the most fatigue on days two and three.

Cold water held soreness down on the first day, but it climbed on the second before easing on the third.

“It is notable to recognize that these responses did not result in significantly greater recovery of muscle strength or lower levels of soreness over the following 72 hours,” Bayne noted.

The study tested a single session of each treatment, and the authors said one session may not capture what repeated use does.

Recent findings suggest that the team didn’t track what the volunteers ate, and only asked them to state their first day’s meals. Soreness ratings were filled in online, and only 29 of the 40 people completed every one.

In a recent development, with nine women among 40 people, the team couldn’t ask whether men and women respond differently to heat and cold. And the blood marker for muscle damage is an indirect one, since no muscle tissue was sampled.

It has been revealed that bayne’s team wants larger groups, repeated exposures, and tests of timing and dose. “Further research is needed to understand whether repeated exposure to heat-based recovery strategies might produce longer-term benefits,” she remarked.

Until that work is done, heat changes the blood in ways cold does not, and the strength tests show no difference in recovery between them.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Thermal Biology.

A upcoming AI tool could help fight online wildlife trafficking

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have developed a way to recognize elephant ivory, pangolin scales, and tiger claws in photographs to help investigators flag suspicious online listings.
  • A latest AI tool can identify elephant, pangolin, and tiger products in photographs, even among similar-looking everyday objects.
  • Tests suggest it could help investigators sift through online listings and decide which items deserve closer inspection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have developed a way to recognize elephant ivory, pangolin scales, and tiger claws in photographs to help investigators flag suspicious online listings.

A latest AI tool can identify elephant, pangolin, and tiger products in photographs, even among similar-looking everyday objects.

Tests suggest it could help investigators sift through online listings and decide which items deserve closer inspection.

The research was led by Enrico Di Minin at the University of Helsinki. Lead author Ritwik Kulkarni worked with the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) on the image library and prototype.

Wildlife products change appearance as they become jewelry, ornaments, or medicines. A photograph may show a carved bracelet, loose scales, or a claw, with few clues about its origin.

Sources indicate that illegal and unsustainable trade contributes to wildlife declines. Tracking it online means reviewing large numbers of photographs across shopping sites and social media, often with limited staff.

“Identifying illegal wildlife products, such as elephant ivory, using AI was one of the grand challenges we were facing,” Di Minin stated.

“These new tools offer novel opportunities for real-time monitoring of online illegal trade in ivory, pangolin scales, and tiger claws for enforcement purposes.”.

The researchers assembled 39,941 images collected through IFAW’s monitoring work in China between 2008 and 2023.

Sources indicate that sources included online advertisements, market inspections, publicly reported seizures, and image searches. This gave the team examples of products as they actually appeared in trade-related photographs.

The library also included objects that could fool a reviewer. Jade bracelets resembled ivory bracelets, while slices of herbal medicine looked like pangolin scales.

Two experienced IFAW analysts reviewed the labels and resolved disagreements. Objects were also marked with boxes, teaching the model where to look within each photograph.

That mattered for crowded product displays and collages. The system needed to locate a suspicious item even when other objects appeared beside it.

The team compared models trained separately for each target group with a model trained on all three. The combined approach performed best overall.

“The best model achieved an overall accuracy of 84% and exceeded 90% accuracy for tiger and pangolin products,” Kulkarni remarked.

The paper gives the figures as 93.6% for pangolin products and 90.3% for tiger products. Elephant products proved harder, with an accuracy of 71.1%.

Industry observers note that ivory carvings can resemble objects made from bone or resin. The researchers also noted that models may sometimes rely on surrounding visual clues instead of the object’s identifying features.

“When integrated into a research prototype smartphone application and evaluated independently, the tool reached 91.3% accuracy in practical screening tests, highlighting the potential of automated image analysis to help prioritise suspect content for human review,” Kulkarni explained.

The app was assessed using 138 additional images, separately from the initial model tests.

According to recent reports, the prototype lets customers choose an existing photograph or take a new one. It then returns a prediction, with boxes marking the objects it has detected.

According to recent reports, an investigator reviewing online advertisements could submit saved images. During a market inspection, an officer could photograph an item for an initial assessment.

“For these technologies to make a meaningful contribution to conservation, we need to make them accessible and usable by the people working on the ground,” Kulkarni noted.

According to recent reports, “Our prototype demonstrates how we can bridge the gap between AI research and practical conservation applications. An app built on it could help, for example, conservation organizations and authorities.”.

Owners can also give feedback on whether the labels and boxes are correct. That provides a way to record mistakes and improve later versions.

A photograph cannot settle whether a sale is illegal. A flagged image gives investigators something to examine, while qualified authorities remain responsible for legal decisions.

Sources indicate that errors create different problems. False alarms send reviewers toward ordinary goods, while missed detections can leave suspicious listings unnoticed.

Industry observers note that the aim is to help people decide where to spend their time. Specialists would still need to examine the item, the listing, and any other relevant evidence.

Industry observers note that the reported results measure image-recognition performance. They do not show how many illegal sales the tool would prevent or how much it would reduce pressure on wildlife populations.

The researchers initiative to improve accuracy, add more species and products, and explore pilots with conservation organizations and online platforms.

They also want secure, ethical procedures for referring suspected cases to authorities.

Industry observers note that continued training will matter because products and their presentation change. A system built from past photographs needs updating as latest examples enter the market.

The paper also suggests combining images with information from listing text. That could help when a photograph alone leaves too much uncertainty.

“We are excited to see this research translate into a practical screening tool for combating illegal online wildlife trade,” stated Lionel Hachemin, IFAW’s Wildlife Crime Program Director.

“This study demonstrates what’s possible when conservation organizations and researchers join forces. We see this as a practical step toward turning the tide on illegal wildlife trade online.”.

The study is published in the journal Conservation Biology.
